selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality, single- vs multi-profile input, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor in the search space. It uses both modalities, multiprofile input, the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat), a mid-range RNA encoder (scVI) and the generally stronger image backbone (ViT-L). It gives a reasonable estimate of achievable performance without committing to the more complex transformer or weighted-fusion options. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Every later experiment can change one factor from this anchor. Dropping a modality, switching to singleprofile, changing an encoder, or trying transformer aggregation or weighted fusion would each attribute a performance change to a single design decision. This is more informative per experiment than starting from a corner of the space such as the simplest unimodal baseline.

Evidence: we have only one result. The multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l model with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. One run cannot tell us whether combining modalities helps or which modality drives performance. Test: config_005 is the RNA-only version of the same setup (same scvi_n200 encoder, multiprofile, avgpool). Changing only the modality isolates how much of the 0.332 comes from RNA alone and how much the image branch and fusion add. Why now: modality is the most basic design choice, and most of the remaining search space (36 of 51 configurations) is multimodal. Knowing early whether the image branch adds value tells us whether to keep spending budget on image encoders and fusion options or to focus on RNA encoders and aggregation.

Evidence: with the same scVI RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, adding ViT-L image features through concat fusion dropped validation accuracy from 0.635 (RNA-only, config_005) to 0.332 (config_036). F1 fell by a similar amount (0.618 to 0.315). The open question is whether images are uninformative or noisy, or whether naive concat lets the high-dimensional image embedding swamp the RNA signal. Test: config_037 is identical to config_036 except it uses weighted fusion, so it isolates the fusion choice. If accuracy recovers to or above the RNA-only level, fusion is the bottleneck and the weighted multimodal branch is worth exploiting. If it stays low, that points to the image modality or encoder as the problem, and the search can focus on RNA-only variants (encoder, transformer aggregation) or image-encoder checks. Why now: this single controlled change resolves the biggest design uncertainty so far, whether multimodality can help at all. That decides how much of the remaining budget belongs to the large multimodal half of the search space.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (scVI, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.635 accuracy (F1 0.618). Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features to the same setup lowered accuracy, to 0.540 with weighted fusion and 0.332 with concat fusion. So the image branch appears to hurt rather than help, and weighted fusion seems to reduce that damage, likely by down-weighting images. 2. Test: we have no image-only baseline, so we cannot tell whether the image features carry little useful signal or whether the fusion method is the problem. Image-only ViT-L with avgpool uses the same encoder and aggregation as the multimodal runs, so it isolates the image modality's standalone value. 3. Why now: multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. If image-only is near chance, we can drop most multimodal configurations and focus the budget on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it is reasonably strong, fusion design is the bottleneck, and further fusion and aggregation experiments are justified. Either result removes a lot of uncertainty about where to spend the remaining budget.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The single-modality models with avgpool score about 0.63 each (RNA 0.635, image 0.632). Multimodal fusion with avgpool falls well below them: 0.540 with weighted fusion and 0.332 with concat. So weighted fusion beats concat, but fusion as tested hurts rather than helps. It is unclear whether the bottleneck is avgpool aggregation of multiprofile inputs or fusion itself. 2. What this tests: config_039 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_037. It keeps scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l and the better weighted fusion fixed. This is a controlled test of whether a learned set aggregator lets multimodal models match or beat the single-modality baselines. 3. Why it is the best next use: Whether multimodal models can outperform single-modality ones at all is the central question of the study. This one experiment informs both the aggregation choice and whether further multimodal configurations are worth budget. If it improves substantially, transformer aggregation becomes the direction to exploit. If not, the problem points to fusion or encoders, which would redirect the next experiments.

1) Evidence: The two unimodal avgpool baselines are the strongest results so far (RNA-only scVI 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1, image-only ViT-L 0.632 / 0.607). Multimodal fusion has not beaten either one. Concat did badly (0.33), weighted did better (0.54), and switching avgpool to transformer aggregation raised weighted-fusion multimodal from 0.54 to 0.59, with F1 rising alongside it. 2) Test: config_006 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This shows whether the transformer gain carries over to a unimodal model or depends on the multimodal setting. 3) Value: it is a one-variable change from the current best result, so it is the most likely next step to set a new top accuracy. Either way, it tells us whether aggregation is a major design lever, which affects how we should prioritize the many remaining multimodal and image-only configurations.

1) Evidence so far: the best results come from unimodal avgpool models, RNA-only scVI at 0.635 and image-only ViT-L at 0.632. Every multimodal fusion tried with scVI plus ViT-L has done worse than either single modality: concat 0.33, weighted 0.54, weighted with transformer 0.59. For RNA, avgpool also beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.599). The biggest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder, since only scVI has been tested and pca_n2000 and scGPT are unexplored. 2) This experiment swaps scVI for scGPT and keeps everything else matched to the current best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). Comparing it directly with config_005 shows whether the choice of RNA representation matters, and whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3) This is the best use of the next run because it isolates one high-impact, untested design choice inside a strong, well-understood baseline. More multimodal fusion runs look risky given their consistent underperformance. The result will also guide which RNA encoder to carry into any later multimodal or aggregation experiments.

1) Evidence: the best results so far are unimodal multiprofile models with avgpool: RNA-only scVI at 0.635 and image-only ViT-L at 0.632. Multimodal fusion has not beaten either. Weighted fusion beats concat, and transformer aggregation helped weighted fusion but slightly hurt RNA-only. scGPT was weaker than scVI. However, every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so we do not yet know whether multiprofile aggregation itself adds value. 2) This experiment runs RNA-only scVI in the singleprofile setting. It is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best, config_005, and shows how much the profile setting matters. 3) The profile setting is a major untested design axis that conditions how we read every aggregation and fusion result. A single controlled run on the strongest encoder resolves it efficiently. That is a better use of the budget than another small fusion or aggregation variant.

1. Evidence: The single-modality baselines are strong and similar: scVI RNA-only reaches 0.635 and ViT image-only reaches 0.632 (multiprofile, avgpool). Every multimodal run tested so far has done worse than either baseline: concat 0.33, weighted 0.54, transformer+weighted 0.59. These failures all used multiprofile aggregation. For RNA-only, single-profile (0.619) was close to multiprofile (0.635), so aggregation is not obviously needed. 2. Question: This run uses the best encoder pair (scVI + ViT-L) with the better fusion method (weighted) in the single-profile setting, with no aggregation. It tests whether the multimodal shortfall comes from fusion itself or from how fusion interacts with multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why now: This is the largest unresolved question in the study. If single-profile multimodal beats about 0.635, there is a clear new direction to exploit. If it also falls short, that points to fusion as the bottleneck, and remaining runs should go to single-modality refinements. Filling in config_038 (transformer+concat) would only refine a fusion method that already looks weak.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_035 (singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It beats every RNA-only and image-only run, so singleprofile multimodal with weighted fusion looks like the promising region. Two other questions already have some evidence. On fusion, weighted clearly beat concat in multiprofile (0.54 vs 0.33). On RNA encoder, scvi beat scgpt (0.635 vs 0.530). The image encoder, however, has never been varied: every image run so far used imagenet_vit_l, and resnet50 is completely untested. 2) What this tests: config_029 keeps the best setup and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This gives a clean one-factor comparison against config_035. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: the image encoder choice affects about half of the remaining configurations, so resolving it is worth more than a fusion test (config_034), where the evidence already favours weighted. Because it stays in the best-performing region, it also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about whether combining RNA and image data helps, whether using multiple profiles helps, or which encoders and fusion methods work best. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-complexity multimodal anchor: scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile input, average pooling and concat fusion. scVI is a common, efficient RNA representation, and avgpool and concat are the simplest choices for aggregation and fusion. It gives a reasonably strong first baseline whose result can later be compared one factor at a time with RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031) and other encoders. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Starting from a central point in the design space makes each later experiment a clean single-variable comparison. It also has a fair chance of performing well right away, which balances learning about the design space with finding a good configuration.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1. We have no reference point yet, so we cannot tell whether the image branch adds value. 2. Test: config_005 removes only the image modality and keeps the same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This single-factor ablation directly measures how much the resnet50 image branch contributes. 3. Why now: Most of the search space is multimodal, so knowing early whether fusion beats RNA alone decides where the remaining budget should go. If multimodal clearly wins, later experiments can focus on image encoder, aggregation and fusion choices. If not, they should prioritise RNA encoder and aggregation.

1) Evidence: with the scVI-n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion dropped accuracy sharply, from 0.650 (RNA-only) to 0.422. F1 fell by a similar amount (0.628 to 0.405). That is a large gap, not noise. It is still unclear whether the image modality is harmful in itself or whether naive concatenation lets weak or noisy image features swamp the RNA signal. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) and holds the RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed. It therefore cleanly tests whether learned modality weighting can recover or exceed RNA-only performance. 3) Fusion is a key design axis across all 24 multimodal configurations remaining. Settling whether weighted fusion fixes the multimodal deficit tells us whether to keep investing in multimodal setups or pivot toward RNA-only variants, such as different encoders or transformer aggregation. A one-variable comparison against an existing result makes it the most informative use of the next run.

Evidence: with scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, concat fusion did poorly (0.422 acc), while weighted fusion reached 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1. That is only marginally better than RNA-only avgpool (0.650 / 0.628). So weighted fusion clearly beats concat, but the image branch adds little so far. Aggregation is a major untested structural choice: every multiprofile run used avgpool, and transformer aggregation has never been tried. Test: config_033 changes only aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to the current best (config_031). This isolates whether learned set aggregation over profiles improves on mean pooling. Why now: the answer applies to all multiprofile configurations, whichever encoders are used. It also exploits the best-known fusion choice, so it has good odds of a new best while resolving a key uncertainty. Encoder swaps (scGPT, ViT-L) remain good follow-ups once the aggregation choice is settled.

1) Evidence so far: with scVI RNA features, ResNet50 image features and multiprofile input, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.653 vs 0.422 accuracy). Avgpool aggregation also beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.653 vs 0.507). However, the best multimodal result is essentially tied with RNA-only (0.653/0.628 vs 0.650/0.628 accuracy/F1). So with ResNet50, the image branch adds almost nothing, and the value of the image encoder is the main open question. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and changes only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. That cleanly tests whether a stronger image representation lets multimodal fusion outperform RNA-only. 3) Changing one factor relative to the current best builds on the strongest evidence while resolving a key uncertainty. A gain would point the search toward ViT-L multimodal configurations. No gain would suggest the RNA encoder is the more important lever, and the next step would be comparing scGPT and PCA.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: Every run so far has used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Within that setting, three patterns are fairly consistent. Weighted fusion strongly beats concat (0.653 vs 0.422). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.653 vs 0.507). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.653 vs 0.586). The best multimodal run (config_031) is only slightly better than RNA-only scVI (0.650), so the RNA representation appears to drive most of the performance. The RNA encoder choice is also the largest design axis we have not yet tested. 2) What this tests: Swapping scVI for scGPT while keeping the best-performing pipeline (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding improves accuracy and F1. 3) Why this is the best next run: It explores a major untested factor while exploiting the strongest known setup, so it could either produce a new best configuration or confirm that scVI is the right RNA encoder to keep for further refinement.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Within the multiprofile setting, several choices look settled for now. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.653 vs 0.422). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.653 vs 0.507). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.586). scVI is slightly ahead of scGPT (0.632). However, every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a major design choice we have not tested at all. 2) What this tests: config_029 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, where aggregation does not apply. Compared directly with config_031, it shows whether aggregating multiple profiles helps or whether a single profile does as well. 3) Why it is the best use of the next experiment: it is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best on a high-impact, completely unexplored dimension. Whichever way it comes out, it decides whether the rest of the budget should go to multiprofile aggregation variants or to the simpler singleprofile branch. It also keeps the strongest known components, so it has a reasonable chance of performing competitively.

1. Evidence: the best multimodal run, config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, 0.653 accuracy), barely beats RNA-only scVI with avgpool, config_005 (0.650). This suggests the RNA representation carries most of the signal. Within this pipeline, the choices that have been varied each lowered performance: concat fusion (0.42), transformer aggregation (0.51), single-profile input (0.54) and ViT-L in place of ResNet50 (0.59). Swapping scVI for scGPT changed little (0.632). The PCA_n2000 RNA encoder has never been tested, so the RNA encoder is the least-explored design choice that seems to matter most. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best pipeline (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps in PCA_n2000. It is a one-variable comparison against config_031 (scVI) and config_043 (scGPT). It will show whether a simple high-dimensional PCA input matches or beats the learned embeddings, using accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: it fills the largest remaining gap on the most influential factor while staying inside the strongest known setup. That makes it both exploratory and plausibly competitive. The result will also tell us whether the remaining PCA-based configurations are worth spending budget on.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best multimodal result (config_031, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) is essentially tied with RNA-only scVI (config_005; 0.650 / 0.628). Concat fusion collapsed to 0.422. Together this suggests weighted fusion may simply be down-weighting the image branch. No image-only baseline exists yet, so we do not know whether images carry useful signal at all. 2. What this tests: Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (config_011) mirrors the best setup's image branch. It directly measures how much signal the image modality has on its own. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: If image-only performance is weak, future experiments should focus on the RNA side (encoders such as scGPT vs scVI, and aggregation). If it is reasonably strong, the near-zero fusion gain means fusion design is the bottleneck and worth exploring. This one experiment resolves a key uncertainty that shapes the rest of the search, rather than adding another small variation to the multimodal grid.

1. Evidence: The best multimodal run (config_031, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) is essentially tied with RNA-only scVI (config_005, 0.650 / 0.628). Image-only is weak (0.421). This suggests the image modality adds little, but that conclusion rests on a single paired comparison. scGPT is the second-strongest RNA encoder, at 0.632 in the weighted multimodal setting. 2. Test: Running scGPT RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool creates a second matched RNA-only vs multimodal pair (against config_043). It shows whether adding images helps, hurts or does nothing for a different RNA encoder. It also gives a clean scGPT vs scVI comparison in the RNA-only setting. 3. Why now: Whether the image branch matters is the most consequential open design question, since it decides whether the remaining budget should go to image and fusion variants or to RNA-side choices. This experiment checks that conclusion while staying close to the current best region, so it may also be competitive on accuracy.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about any design choice: modality, single vs. multi-profile, encoders, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is a central reference point. Each design choice can be isolated later by changing one factor at a time: RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), or a different encoder (config_018, config_036, config_042). 3) A plausible, mid-complexity configuration used as this hub makes every later experiment a clean one-factor comparison. That gets the most learning per experiment under the limited budget, while still having a reasonable chance of good accuracy.

1. Evidence: only one result exists. The multimodal model (scVI RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.435 accuracy and 0.423 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell how much of that comes from the image branch versus the RNA representation. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the same scVI encoder, the same multiprofile avgpool setup and the same aggregation, but removes images. It is a clean one-factor test of whether adding imaging improves accuracy. 3. Why now: modality is the highest-level design choice and decides how to spend the remaining budget. If RNA-only scores about the same, image encoder and fusion variants (ViT-L, weighted fusion) are unlikely to pay off, and effort should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it clearly drops, that confirms the multimodal direction and justifies exploring image encoders and fusion next.

Evidence: the multimodal scVI+ResNet50 avgpool concat model (0.435 acc, 0.423 F1) far outperforms the matched RNA-only model (0.208 acc). That gap suggests most of the signal may come from the image modality. What is still unknown is whether fusion adds anything beyond images alone. Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool completes a clean modality ablation, since every other setting matches the two runs already done. If it scores close to 0.435, the image encoder is the main driver, and the next budget should go to image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion type. If it scores clearly lower, RNA contributes complementary signal, and further searching over multimodal fusion and RNA encoders is justified. This single run decides where in the large multimodal grid the remaining budget is best spent.

1. Evidence: Image features carry most of the signal. Image-only reached 0.421 accuracy, while RNA-only (scVI) reached only 0.208. Multimodal concat improved slightly on image-only, to 0.435 accuracy and 0.423 F1. This suggests RNA adds a small amount and the image representation is the main performance lever. Only ResNet50 has been tested, so the image encoder choice is the largest open question. 2. Test: This run changes one factor from the current best (config_030), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. scVI, multiprofile, avgpool and concat stay fixed, so any difference can be attributed to the image encoder. 3. Why now: Because images dominate performance, the encoder choice is likely to matter most. This experiment both reduces uncertainty about an important design choice and could plausibly beat the current best. Aggregation, fusion and the RNA encoder are better tested after the image backbone is settled.

1. Evidence: The image encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the same multimodal scVI/avgpool/concat setup raised accuracy from 0.435 to 0.725, with F1 rising in step from 0.423 to 0.685. RNA alone is weak (0.208), and adding it to ResNet50 gave only a small gain over image-only (0.435 vs 0.421). Aggregation has never been varied; every multiprofile run used avgpool. 2. Test: config_038 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging when the image features are strong. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a major untested design axis. Testing it on the strongest backbone is both informative and likely to perform well. Fusion type, RNA encoder choice and an image-only ViT-L ablation can follow once we know the better aggregator.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is a large jump over the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.435). But RNA-only scVI is weak (0.208), and with ResNet50, adding RNA barely beat image-only (0.435 vs 0.421). So it is unclear whether the gain comes from multimodal fusion or almost entirely from the ViT-L image encoder. 2) Test: Image-only ViT-L with avgpool differs from config_036 only by removing RNA. This isolates the RNA contribution when the image encoder is strong. 3) Why now: The answer decides how to spend the remaining budget. If ViT-L alone matches 0.725, RNA encoder and fusion choices matter little, and we should focus on image-side and aggregation choices. If it falls clearly short, RNA adds value, and exploring alternative RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) and weighted fusion around config_036 becomes the priority. It is also a plausible high performer in its own right.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is far above image-only ViT-L (0.485) and the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.435), so the ViT-L multimodal avgpool direction looks strong. Transformer aggregation dropped accuracy sharply (0.332), so avgpool is the better choice for now. Fusion is the main gap: every multimodal run used concat, so we know nothing about weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_037 changes only concat to weighted on the best configuration. This isolates whether the fusion method matters, and it is a plausible way to improve on 0.725. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while settling a design choice that applies to every multimodal configuration. Whichever fusion wins can guide later RNA-encoder comparisons (scGPT, PCA) without confounding them with fusion.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. It clearly beats the image-only ViT-L run (0.485), which suggests the RNA signal helps once it is fused. Changing one factor at a time from config_036 lowered performance when aggregation became transformer (0.332) and when fusion became weighted (0.494). So avgpool plus concat looks like a strong backbone, though each comparison is still a single run. The main untested choice is the RNA encoder: every RNA run so far used scVI, and scVI alone was weak (0.208). Test: config_048 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only scVI for scGPT. This isolates the RNA encoder effect where it matters most. Why now: it is both a sensible exploitation step (scGPT is a pretrained foundation encoder that might improve on 0.725) and the best way to reduce uncertainty about a design axis with no data yet. That makes it a better use of budget than revisiting aggregation or fusion, which already have some evidence.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-factor changes from it all hurt badly: transformer aggregation (0.332), weighted fusion (0.494) and the scGPT encoder (0.227). Every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so the singleprofile option has never been tested. That makes profile setting the largest remaining uncertainty among the major design choices. Test: config_034 keeps the best RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion method, and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether single-profile inputs do as well or better. The transformer-aggregation result hints that aggregation can hurt. Why now: it is a controlled one-factor comparison against the current best. Either it finds a better configuration or it confirms multiprofile+avgpool as the right choice and rules out half of the remaining search space. That is more informative per experiment than further fusion or encoder tweaks. Swapping in the PCA RNA encoder (config_024) is the natural next test after this.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-factor changes from it have each been tested and all lowered performance. Transformer aggregation gave 0.33, weighted fusion 0.49, the scGPT RNA encoder 0.23, and single-profile 0.52. The one main design axis still unexplored is the PCA (n2000) RNA encoder, which has never been tried in any setting. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the RNA encoder in config_036, from scVI to PCA. This shows whether scVI is specifically responsible for the strong multimodal gain, or whether any reasonable RNA representation combined with ViT-L, avgpool and concat works well. The large scGPT drop suggests the RNA encoder choice matters a lot. 3. Why now: This is a controlled one-factor comparison against the current best configuration. It closes the last untested RNA encoder option and has a real chance of matching or beating the best result. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than retesting axes that have already shown clear losses.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about which design choices matter. The open questions are whether multimodal fusion helps, which encoders are best, and whether multiprofile aggregation beats a single profile. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-range multimodal anchor using simple, commonly strong components: scvi_n200 for RNA, resnet50 for images, multiprofile avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result sets a baseline from which single factors can be changed in later runs (unimodal, encoder swaps, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, single profile). This gives clean ablations instead of scattered comparisons. 3. Why it is the best first run: It has reasonable odds of performing well, since it combines both modalities with multiple profiles using simple choices less likely to overfit. It also sits at the center of the design space, so each following experiment can isolate one decision. That makes it a sensible way to start under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists, config_030 (multimodal, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat). It reached 0.527 accuracy and 0.510 F1. One result gives no basis for judging which design choice drives performance. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes a single factor from that baseline by removing the image branch, keeping the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Comparing the two isolates how much the imaging modality adds over RNA alone. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion beats unimodal is the most important early question, because it decides whether much of the search space is worth pursuing. If RNA-only matches the baseline, later budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it drops clearly, the next experiments should go to image encoders and fusion strategies. This one-factor test reduces more uncertainty than tuning a secondary choice like aggregation or fusion type at this stage.

Evidence: with the same scVI encoder and avgpool aggregation, the concat multimodal model (config_030, accuracy 0.527, F1 0.510) scored below RNA-only (config_005, accuracy 0.573, F1 0.573). This suggests that naively adding ResNet50 image features may hurt, but one comparison is weak evidence. It is unclear whether the fault lies with the image modality itself or with the concat fusion strategy. Test: config_031 is identical to config_030 except it uses weighted fusion. This isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion closes the gap or beats RNA-only, the image modality is recoverable and fusion is the key lever. If it still underperforms, the image features themselves are likely the problem, which would point toward an image encoder or image-only check next. Why now: fusion is a design choice that affects half of all remaining multimodal configurations. A controlled one-variable comparison therefore reduces the most uncertainty per experiment while keeping a realistic chance of beating the current best.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.573 accuracy / 0.573 F1) clearly beats both multimodal scVI+ResNet50 runs (about 0.52-0.53). Concat and weighted fusion performed almost identically, so fusion type appears unimportant here. Adding ResNet50 image features seems to hurt rather than help. The RNA pathway is therefore the strongest lever so far, but only one RNA encoder (scVI) has been tested. 2) This run swaps scVI for scGPT and keeps everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). That isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Encoder choice is a major untested factor, and it will shape every later multimodal comparison. Transformer aggregation (0.494) and singleprofile (0.260) were much worse. Adding images has not beaten RNA-only: the best multimodal run, resnet50 with weighted fusion, reached 0.688, and image-only resnet50 reached only 0.485. The main remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder, because pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2) This experiment tests pca_n2000 in the best-performing template (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). Since that template is fixed, any change can be attributed to the encoder alone. 3) This is a good use of the budget because it closes the largest untested gap with a single run and could produce a new best. It also tells us whether later multimodal pca runs (config_018 or config_019) are worth spending experiments on.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool is clearly the strongest design. The top results are RNA-only scVI (0.713) and RNA-only scGPT (0.706). With the scVI/resnet50 pairing, weighted fusion beat concat (0.688 vs 0.635). Even so, the best multimodal run is still below RNA-only, so whether adding images helps at all is unresolved. Transformer aggregation and ViT-L both performed poorly in their single tests, so they are less promising for now. 2. Test: config_043 uses the best-known multimodal recipe (resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) with scGPT instead of scVI. It checks whether the weighted-fusion advantage holds for a second strong RNA encoder. It also checks whether scGPT pairs better with image features, possibly enough to beat RNA-only. 3. Value: This changes one factor in the best multimodal setup, so the result is easy to interpret. It could find a new best, and if it does not, it strengthens the case for focusing on RNA-only settings. Either outcome is more useful than exploring areas that already look weak.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters for this task. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple anchor point. It uses multimodal input, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, concat fusion, and the simplest encoders (pca_n2000 and resnet50). It shows whether a basic multimodal, multi-profile model works well without adding the extra complexity of transformer aggregation, weighted fusion or pretrained foundation encoders. Later experiments can change one factor at a time from this baseline: single vs. multi profile (config_016), unimodal ablations (config_002, config_011), avgpool vs. transformer (config_020), concat vs. weighted (config_019), and stronger encoders (config_030, config_024, config_042). 3. Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting at the extremes, such as an unimodal single-profile model or the most complex scGPT/ViT/transformer setup, would give a less useful reference. A mid-complexity anchor gives a reasonable chance of good accuracy and the most interpretable comparisons for the experiments that follow.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) gave a baseline of 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Every design choice is still uncertain. 2. Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean estimate of whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3. Why now: Aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, unimodal and multimodal, so the answer narrows a large part of the search space. A one-factor change against the existing baseline makes the result directly interpretable. It also has a reasonable chance of improving performance, so it balances learning about the design space with improving the best result. Comparisons of encoders, fusion method and modality can then use the better aggregator.

1) Evidence: with everything else fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 10 points in both accuracy (0.619 vs 0.520) and F1 (0.610 vs 0.479). That is a large, consistent gap, so it is reasonable to keep transformer aggregation as the working baseline, though it rests on a single pair of runs. Encoder choice, fusion and profile setting are all still untested. 2) Test: config_044 changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to the pretrained scGPT, keeping the best configuration so far. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation adds value beyond PCA. 3) Why now: the encoder axis has the most options and plausibly the largest effect. Changing one factor from the current best both exploits the transformer result and gives a clean answer on an important design choice. Fusion type (config_021) and image encoder (config_026) are natural follow-ups.

1. Evidence: Two single-factor comparisons point the same way. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.10 accuracy and 0.13 F1 (config_020 vs config_018). scGPT beat PCA by about 0.11 accuracy and 0.07 F1 (config_044 vs config_020). Each rests on one comparison, but the gaps are large and consistent across both metrics. The image encoder and the fusion method have not been varied at all; every run so far used ResNet50 with concat. 2. Test: config_050 keeps the current best setup (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of the image backbone, an untested design choice that may matter a lot. 3. Why now: It explores a major uncertain factor while staying in the most promising region, so it could also improve on the current best. Fusion type is likely a smaller effect and is better tested once the image encoder choice is resolved.

Evidence: Four experiments, all using concat fusion, point to transformer aggregation (+0.10 accuracy over avgpool with PCA/ResNet50), scGPT RNA embeddings (+0.11 over PCA) and ResNet50 over ViT-L (+0.05 with scGPT/transformer). The best so far is config_044 at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Fusion strategy has never been varied, so it is the largest remaining uncertainty among the multimodal design choices. What it tests: config_045 keeps the best configuration fixed and switches only concat to weighted fusion. This gives a clean one-factor test of whether fusion matters. Why now: it explores an untested axis while staying in the most promising region, so it may also improve on the best result. If weighted fusion helps, later runs can extend it to other settings. If it does not, concat can be fixed and the budget moved to unimodal baselines, such as scGPT RNA-only with transformer aggregation, to measure what the images contribute.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, accuracy 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-variable comparisons favor transformer over avgpool aggregation (+0.10 with PCA), scGPT over PCA (+0.11), ResNet50 over ViT-L (+0.05), and concat over weighted fusion (+0.14). The scVI_n200 RNA encoder has never been tested, so its effect is the largest open uncertainty about the RNA encoder, which has so far been the factor with the biggest impact. 2) Test: config_032 swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI and keeps the best-known ResNet50, transformer and concat settings. This gives a clean comparison against config_044 (scGPT) and config_020 (PCA), completing the RNA-encoder comparison under the strongest settings. 3) Value: It covers an untested option of a high-impact design choice and still has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than further fusion or aggregation variants, whose effects already have consistent supporting evidence.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The history points to several robust patterns. The RNA encoder matters most: scGPT beats PCA (0.619), which beats scVI (0.427). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.620 vs 0.520 with PCA). Concat fusion beats weighted (0.725 vs 0.586). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.725 vs 0.678). The key untested question is whether the image modality adds anything at all. Every run so far has been multimodal, and the large swings from changing the RNA encoder suggest RNA may carry most of the signal. 2. Test: config_009 is the RNA-only version of the best setup (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer). It directly measures the image branch's contribution. If it matches or beats 0.725, multimodality is not helping, and the remaining budget should shift toward RNA-side choices. If it falls clearly below, the image branch is earning its place, and further image or fusion tuning is justified. 3. Why now: This one ablation resolves the most basic open design decision (modality setting), which affects how the rest of the budget is spent. It also has a realistic chance of matching the current best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

1) Evidence: The other design choices have each been compared at least once, all within the multiprofile setting. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.62 vs 0.52 with PCA). scGPT was the best RNA encoder (0.72, vs 0.62 for PCA and 0.43 for scVI). ResNet50 beat ViT-L (0.72 vs 0.68). Concat fusion beat weighted fusion (0.72 vs 0.59). Multimodal far exceeded RNA-only (0.72 vs 0.33). Profile setting has never been varied, so whether multiprofile modeling is needed is the largest open question about a core design choice. 2) Test: config_040 takes the current best stack (scGPT + ResNet50 + concat) and switches it to the single-profile setting. Comparing it with config_044 isolates the effect of multiprofile modeling with transformer aggregation. 3) Why now: This contrast fills the one untested dimension, anchored to the strongest configuration so far. A large drop would confirm multiprofile as essential and justify focusing the remaining budget on refining multiprofile variants. A comparable or better result would open the cheaper single-profile branch (configs 016, 022, 028, 046, etc.) for further search.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer, concat; 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Matched comparisons favor multiprofile over singleprofile, concat over weighted fusion, ResNet50 over ViT-L, and scGPT over PCA and scVI. The RNA-only scGPT transformer reached only 0.332 accuracy. The unresolved question is how much of the multimodal performance comes from the image branch, because no image-only model has been tested. 2. Test: config_012 is the image-only ResNet50 transformer counterpart of config_044. Comparing them isolates the image modality's contribution and shows how much RNA adds on top of it. If image-only gets close to 0.72, the RNA encoder choice matters less than it appears, and later experiments should focus on image and aggregation choices. If it scores much lower, fusing both modalities is confirmed as essential. 3. Why now: Most remaining multimodal variants change factors that already have consistent, if limited, evidence. This single run instead resolves the modality-attribution question at the top level of the design, so it should guide the rest of the limited budget better than another small refinement near config_044.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Multimodal multiprofile models beat single-profile and unimodal ones. scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder, ResNet50 beat ViT-L, and concat beat weighted fusion. However, the evidence that transformer aggregation beats avgpool comes from one PCA-based pair (0.620 vs 0.520). Aggregation is one of the largest effects observed, yet it has not been checked with the best RNA encoder. 2) Test: config_042 swaps only the aggregation in the best configuration (avgpool instead of transformer). This is a clean one-variable comparison. It shows whether the transformer's advantage holds with scGPT embeddings, or whether richer pretrained RNA features shrink the gap and make the simpler avgpool competitive. 3) Why now: It strengthens or overturns a key design conclusion in the context that matters most, the top-performing backbone. It also has a reasonable chance of matching the best score. That makes it a better use of the budget than configurations that combine already-weaker choices (scVI, weighted fusion) or that test a factor with lower expected impact.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor. It uses both modalities, multiprofile input with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), the simplest fusion (concat), a compact RNA encoder (scVI, 200 dimensions) and a standard image backbone (ResNet50). Each later experiment can change one factor from this point and act as a clean ablation. Examples are dropping to rna_only or image_only, switching to singleprofile, using transformer aggregation or weighted fusion, or upgrading to scGPT or ViT-L. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, an anchor near the middle of the design space is a better first run than a unimodal baseline at the edge or the most complex configuration. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far, the multimodal multiprofile scVI + ResNet50 avgpool concat model (config_030) at 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. A single point cannot tell us whether the image branch and fusion add anything. 2. Test: config_005 removes only the image modality and keeps the same RNA encoder (scVI), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This isolates the contribution of the image modality and multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: whether to be multimodal at all is the highest-level design choice and shapes which other factors are worth searching (image encoder, fusion type, aggregation). A matched one-factor ablation answers it cleanly with one experiment before we spend budget on finer multimodal variations such as ViT-L or transformer aggregation.

1. Evidence: with the same scVI RNA encoder and multiprofile avgpool setup, adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.540, F1 0.524) did much worse than RNA-only (config_005, acc 0.688, F1 0.659). The unresolved question is why: the image modality may simply be uninformative, or naive concatenation may let noisy image features drown out the strong RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only one factor, concat to weighted fusion, keeping everything else identical to config_030. If weighted fusion recovers to or beats RNA-only accuracy, the fusion mechanism caused the drop and multimodal search stays promising. If it stays near 0.54, images (at least ResNet50) are likely hurting. That would point the search toward RNA-only variants or a different image encoder. 3. Why now: fusion type appears in half of the multimodal space, so resolving it early tells us whether the many remaining multimodal configurations are worth the budget. A clean single-variable comparison gives the most interpretable information per experiment.

1. Evidence: RNA-only with scVI and avgpool (config_005) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Adding ResNet50 image features with the same RNA encoder and aggregation dropped performance sharply, to about 0.53 accuracy. This held for both concat and weighted fusion, so the drop is consistent across fusion types. The key uncertainty is why. Either the image modality is generally unhelpful or noisy for this task, or the ResNet50 image encoder specifically gives poor features that swamp the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_036 keeps everything identical to config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, concat) and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a clean one-factor comparison of the image encoder. If ViT-L closes the gap or beats RNA-only, the multimodal branch is still worth pursuing with ViT-L. If it also falls well below 0.688, image fusion looks generally harmful and we can focus the remaining budget on RNA-only choices like encoder and aggregation. 3. Why now: the multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. Learning whether any image encoder can help is the single most budget-relevant question, and it will decide how much of that space deserves further exploration.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1) clearly beats every multimodal run (0.41-0.54), all of which used avgpool. Adding images, especially ViT-L, appears to hurt, and concat versus weighted fusion made little difference. Aggregation is a key choice that remains untested: no transformer-aggregation run exists yet. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. It isolates whether learned multi-profile aggregation improves on simple averaging. 3) It exploits the strongest branch found so far while reducing uncertainty about a factor that applies across the whole search space. The result will guide whether later multimodal or other-encoder runs should use transformer aggregation. It is a more informative single-variable change than another multimodal fusion tweak.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Every multimodal variant scored lower, especially with ViT-L (0.41). Within RNA-only, transformer aggregation dropped to 0.523, so how profiles are aggregated clearly matters. The untested question is whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all compared with a plain single-profile model. Test: config_004 keeps the best RNA-only scVI setup but switches to single-profile. Comparing it directly with config_005 isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation on the strongest branch. Why now: the answer decides whether later budget goes to aggregation variants or to simpler single-profile designs, such as comparing RNA encoders like PCA and scGPT in either setting. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). With scVI held fixed, avgpool beat transformer, multiprofile beat singleprofile, and adding either image encoder lowered performance by a lot (0.41-0.54). The RNA encoder is the main design choice still untested, because every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) This run keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps scVI for scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI in the strongest pipeline found so far. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest evidence while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Adding images (multimodal) and switching to transformer aggregation both cut performance sharply, to roughly 0.41–0.54. Replacing scVI with scGPT under the same RNA-only avgpool setup dropped accuracy to 0.514. The PCA_n2000 RNA encoder is still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the winning RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup and swaps scVI for PCA_n2000. That isolates the RNA encoder choice and shows whether scVI is truly the best representation or whether a simple high-dimensional PCA baseline does as well or better. 3) The RNA encoder is the main unresolved design choice in the strongest part of the search space, so testing it here is the most budget-efficient step. It also has a real chance of beating the current best. Its outcome will guide which encoder to carry into any later multimodal or aggregation experiments.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool is the strongest setting so far. scVI scored 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659) and PCA 0.653. Adding images consistently hurt: scVI+ResNet50 scored 0.54 (concat) and 0.53 (weighted), and scVI+ViT-L scored 0.41. However, no image-only model has been run. So we cannot tell whether the image features carry little signal, or whether the fusion setup is the problem (for example, image noise drowning out the RNA signal). 2) What this tests: an image-only ResNet50 model, using the best-performing multiprofile avgpool setting, directly measures how much predictive signal the image branch carries. If it scores near chance, the remaining budget should focus on RNA-only refinements. If it is reasonably strong, the drop in multimodal runs points to a fusion problem worth investigating further. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: one run resolves the main open question about the image modality and its role in fusion. Extra RNA-only runs would likely give only small gains, since transformer aggregation and scGPT already underperformed.

1. Evidence: Unimodal models do well. The best result is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy). RNA-only PCA (0.653) and image-only ResNet50 (0.639) also perform well, all with avgpool. Multimodal scVI+ResNet50 with avgpool scored well below both of its own unimodal parts, with concat (0.540) and weighted fusion (0.525) about equally poor. Adding ViT-L as the image encoder was worse still (0.411). The key open question is why fusion fails: is it specific to the scVI pairing, or is the multimodal pipeline itself the problem? 2. Test: config_018 keeps everything else from config_030 (ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps the RNA encoder to PCA, the second-strongest RNA representation. If it reaches or beats the unimodal baselines, the fusion failure is specific to the scVI pairing and multimodal search with PCA is worth pursuing. If it also underperforms, the evidence points to a general fusion or optimization problem, and remaining budget should go to unimodal refinement. 3. Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. This controlled one-factor comparison tells us whether to keep exploring that space, so it is worth more than a small exploit on unimodal models.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) This multimodal, multi-profile configuration (scVI RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) serves as a central anchor. It combines the options most likely to perform well (both modalities, multiple profiles, a compact learned RNA embedding, a strong pretrained image backbone) with the simplest aggregation and fusion. 3) Starting from a likely strong but uncomplicated anchor gives a good chance of early performance. Evidence: only one experiment has been run (config_036: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat). It reached 0.427 accuracy and 0.417 F1, so there is no baseline to tell whether this is good or which component drives it. Test: config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder (scVI), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but drops the image modality. Comparing the two isolates how much the ViT-L image branch and concat fusion add over RNA alone. Why now: whether multimodality is worth it is the highest-level design question in this search space. The answer decides whether to spend the remaining budget on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation variants of multimodal models, or to focus on cheaper unimodal ones. A controlled one-factor ablation reduces more uncertainty than a local tweak such as switching to transformer aggregation or weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: Adding ViT-L image features with concat fusion (config_036, acc 0.427, F1 0.417) performed far worse than the matched RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Both use scVI encoding, multiprofile input and avgpool. This gap is too large to be noise. Either the image features hurt, or naive concatenation lets noisy or high-dimensional image features overwhelm the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_037 is identical to config_036 except it uses weighted fusion, so it isolates the fusion choice. If it recovers to near or above 0.72, the fusion method was the problem and multimodal models are worth exploring further. If it stays low, the image modality itself is likely uninformative or harmful, and the search should shift toward RNA-only variants such as encoder and aggregation choices. 3) Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining space. 1. Evidence: RNA-only (scVI, avgpool) reached 0.72 accuracy and 0.68 F1. Both multimodal runs that added the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder fell to about 0.42–0.43, and concat versus weighted fusion made almost no difference. So the drop is not about the fusion choice. It comes either from this particular image encoder or from adding images at all. 2. Test: config_030 keeps everything identical to config_036 (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and changes only the image encoder to ResNet50. Why now: most of the remaining configurations are multimodal, so learning whether that whole branch is salvageable saves the most budget. Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. All three multimodal variants sharing that RNA encoder and aggregation scored far lower (0.42-0.54), so adding image features seems to hurt in this setup. ResNet50 beat ViT-L, and concat and weighted fusion were about the same. Every experiment so far used avgpool, so it is unknown whether transformer aggregation over multiple profiles helps. 1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool is clearly the best so far (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Every multimodal variant has been much worse (0.42–0.54), with ViT-L worse than ResNet50. 1. Evidence: The best result by a wide margin is RNA-only scVI with avgpool multiprofile aggregation (config_005, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Every variant tested so far performs worse. Why now: It resolves the largest untested design axis while staying anchored to the best-known setup, so it has both exploratory value and a real chance of matching or beating the current best. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Why now: it exploits the strongest direction found so far while closing the encoder gap, which also bears on every multimodal configuration that uses PCA. 1) Evidence: The best results so far are unimodal. RNA-only scVI with avgpool reached 0.721 accuracy, and image-only ResNet50 with avgpool reached 0.688. Every multimodal run did worse than either.
