1. Evidence: only one experiment has run. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell which component drives this result, or whether the image branch adds anything. 2. What this tests: config_005 is the matched RNA-only version, with the same scVI-200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and only the image modality removed. The accuracy and F1 difference against config_030 estimates how much the ResNet50 image features contribute. 3. Why now: whether to fuse modalities at all is the highest-level design choice, and it determines whether later budget should go to tuning image encoders and fusion or to RNA encoders and aggregation. 1) Evidence: Multimodal scVI+ResNet50 (avgpool, concat) beat RNA-only scVI by only ~0.6 points in accuracy (0.523 vs 0.518), though F1 rose more (0.508 vs 0.484). The image branch may add a little, but with ResNet50 the benefit is uncertain and could be noise. 2) Test: config_036 keeps everything else fixed and swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is scVI+ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion (0.523 accuracy, 0.508 F1). It is only slightly above RNA-only scVI (0.518 accuracy), although its F1 is clearly higher (0.508 vs 0.484). Swapping in ViT-L under concat fusion dropped accuracy sharply to 0.328. This suggests concat fusion lets a poorly matched image representation hurt performance. It also means it is unclear whether images add real value. Fusion strategy has not been tested at all. 2. Test: This experiment changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, on the current best setup. It shows whether learned modality weighting improves the gain from adding images. 3. Why now: It is a controlled one-factor comparison that both exploits the strongest configuration and settles an important design question. If weighted fusion helps here, it is a strong reason to retry weighted fusion with ViT-L or with transformer aggregation. 1. Evidence: with scvi_n200 and avgpool fixed, the best result so far is resnet50 with concat fusion (0.523 accuracy, 0.508 F1). It is only marginally ahead of RNA-only (0.518), although its F1 is clearly higher. Swapping in ViT-L (0.328) or weighted fusion (0.422) hurt substantially, so those directions look less promising for now. Aggregation is a major design axis that has not been tested at all, since every completed run used avgpool. 2. Test: this run keeps the current best configuration and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It shows whether a learned aggregation over multiple profiles improves on simple pooling, and whether it widens the small multimodal advantage over RNA-only. 3. Why now: it is a single-variable extension of the strongest configuration, so the result is easy to interpret. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All five runs so far used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. The best result is multimodal resnet50 with avgpool and concat (0.523 acc / 0.508 F1). RNA-only scvi is nearly as good (0.518), which suggests the RNA representation drives most of the performance. Switching to the ViT-L image encoder (0.328) or weighted fusion (0.422) clearly hurt. Transformer aggregation was roughly neutral (0.512). The RNA encoder is the biggest untested design choice. 2. What this tests: config_042 changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi to scgpt, while keeping the best known setup (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat). This gives a clean one-factor comparison against config_030 and shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scvi. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Since RNA appears to be the dominant signal, the RNA encoder probably has the largest remaining effect on accuracy. 1. Evidence: All six completed runs used the multiprofile setting. Avgpool was slightly better than transformer aggregation. ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L. The profile setting is the one major design choice with no evidence at all. 2. Test: config_040 keeps the best-performing encoders and concat fusion but switches to singleprofile, which uses no aggregation. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles actually helps. 3. Why now: This one run opens a completely unexplored dimension while staying in the strongest region of the space. It either confirms multiprofile as a design decision or reveals that a simpler setting does as well or better, which would redirect the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: The best result so far, config_040 (scGPT + ResNet50, concat, singleprofile, 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1), beats its multiprofile counterpart config_042 (0.532 / 0.516). That gap is much larger than the other differences seen so far. It is the only paired comparison of profile setting, though, and it uses only the scGPT encoder. Other findings are fairly consistent: ResNet50 beats ViT-L, concat beats weighted fusion, avgpool is about equal to transformer aggregation, and scGPT is roughly equal to scVI under multiprofile (0.532 vs 0.523). 2. Test: config_028 is the singleprofile version of config_030 (scVI + ResNet50, concat). This gives a second paired test of singleprofile versus multiprofile. It shows whether the advantage holds across RNA encoders or depends on scGPT. 3. Why now: Profile setting looks like the most influential design choice. Replicating it before committing the remaining budget to singleprofile variants (fusion, encoder or modality ablations) reduces the risk of overinterpreting one comparison. If the gain holds, the search can focus on singleprofile configurations; if it does not, attention returns to the encoder choice.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_040 (scGPT + ResNet50, single-profile, concat) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. With scVI, the single-profile version did much worse (0.411), so scGPT seems to drive the gain. It is still unclear how much the image branch contributes. RNA-only scVI multi-profile (0.518) nearly matched its multimodal counterpart (0.523), which suggests images add little. Test: scGPT RNA-only single-profile isolates the RNA encoder's contribution in the best-performing setting and shows whether multimodal fusion adds value beyond scGPT. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_040 (scGPT + ResNet50, singleprofile, concat fusion) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. scGPT is consistently stronger than scVI, and ResNet50 beats ViT-L. This isolates the fusion choice in the most promising region of the search space and checks whether the earlier weighted-fusion penalty holds generally or was specific to scVI. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Fusion type splits roughly half of the remaining multimodal configurations, so clarifying it narrows the space efficiently. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design factor is uncertain: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, low-complexity anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, using the simplest components on each axis: PCA RNA features, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result sets a reference point. Later single-factor changes can then be compared against it: rna_only (config_002), image_only (config_011), singleprofile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and swapping in scVI/scGPT or ViT-L encoders. 3. 1. Evidence: We have one result so far. config_018 (multimodal, PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell which parts of the design are driving that performance. 2. Test: config_002 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool) but removes the image branch. This is a controlled one-factor ablation. Why now: Whether to use both modalities is the most basic design choice in this search space. Evidence: with pca_n2000, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, the multimodal concat model (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1) beat the RNA-only model (0.619 acc, 0.610 F1) by about 6 points. We do not yet know whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features being strong by themselves. Test: config_011 is the image-only counterpart (resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool). It changes only the modality and completes the three-way comparison. Why now: if image-only matches or beats multimodal, the search should focus on image encoders such as ViT-L and aggregation, and RNA encoder variants matter less. If it falls clearly below multimodal, the modalities are complementary, and fusion and RNA encoder choices deserve more of the budget. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: multimodal concat fusion (config_018, acc 0.678, F1 0.646) beats RNA-only (0.619) and image-only (0.421). So fusion helps, but the ResNet50 image branch is weak on its own. None of the other design axes have been tested yet: image encoder, RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion type. 2. Why it is the best use of the budget: the image branch is clearly the bottleneck and has the most room to improve. 1) Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Single-factor changes from it have each hurt performance: ViT-L image encoder (0.328), weighted fusion (0.540), transformer aggregation (0.332), scVI RNA encoder (0.536) and single-profile (0.507). Evidence: adding ViT-L image features with concat fusion (config_036, acc 0.208, F1 0.172) roughly halved performance compared with the otherwise identical RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.435, F1 0.423). It is unclear whether this drop means the image modality is uninformative or harmful, or whether naive concatenation is the problem. For example, the high-dimensional ViT-L features may swamp the scVI embedding. Test: config_037 changes only the fusion (concat to weighted) and keeps the RNA encoder, image encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation fixed. If accuracy recovers to near or above the RNA-only level, the fusion method was the bottleneck and multimodal search remains promising. If it stays low, the image features are likely the issue, and the budget should shift toward RNA-only variants or image-only checks. Why now: this single-variable comparison resolves the largest open uncertainty, whether multimodal fusion is viable at all. That answer determines how to spend the remaining budget across roughly 36 multimodal configurations.

1. Evidence: Fusion choice matters a lot. With scVI + ViT-L + avgpool, weighted fusion (0.527 accuracy, 0.510 F1) far outperformed concat (0.208 accuracy) and beat RNA-only (0.435 accuracy). Weighted fusion therefore looks like the right way to add the image modality. Aggregation is still completely untested: every run so far used avgpool. 2. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, weighted) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles adds to the strong weighted-fusion result. 3. Why now: it builds directly on the best configuration while resolving an important open design choice in one clean comparison. That makes it both a likely high performer and an informative experiment for the limited budget. Encoder swaps (ResNet50, PCA, scGPT) can follow once the best aggregation is known.

1) Evidence: with scVI and ViT-L fixed, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527 vs 0.208). Avgpool also beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.527 vs 0.421). The best multimodal model also beat the RNA-only scVI baseline (0.435), and F1 follows the same pattern. Fusion and aggregation therefore look fairly settled, but the RNA encoder has not been varied at all. 2) This experiment keeps the best recipe (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) The RNA encoder is a major untested axis, and RNA alone already carries strong signal. A one-variable change on the best configuration can either find a better model or confirm scVI, which narrows a large part of the remaining search space within the limited budget.

1) Evidence so far: weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527 vs 0.208). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.527 vs 0.421). scGPT and scVI RNA encoders performed about the same (0.537 vs 0.527), and multimodal weighted fusion beat RNA-only (0.435). The image encoder has never been varied, since every multimodal run used imagenet_vit_l. 2) This run keeps the current best setup (scGPT, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50, so any change can be attributed to the encoder. 3) The image encoder is the largest remaining untested design choice. A single-factor change from the best configuration either confirms vit_l or reveals a better encoder, which makes it the most informative use of the next run.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527 vs 0.208 with scvi_n200 + ViT-L), and avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one comparison so far. The current best is scgpt + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1, well above scgpt + ViT-L at 0.537. However, the resnet50 advantage comes from a single comparison within scgpt, so it could be a scgpt-specific interaction rather than a general image-encoder effect. 2. Test: config_031 keeps the winning recipe (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and swaps scgpt for scvi_n200 with resnet50. It completes a 2x2 design (scvi or scgpt by ViT-L or resnet50) under fixed aggregation and fusion. This shows whether resnet50 reliably beats ViT-L. It also gives a cleaner estimate of whether scgpt beats scvi_n200, which looked only slightly better with ViT-L (0.537 vs 0.527). 3. Why now: Confirming a major design factor across two RNA encoders reduces the risk of overfitting to one result. It also keeps the experiment within the most promising region, so it may perform well too. That makes it a better use of budget than less-supported transformer or concat variants.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. It beats every other tested combination by more than 0.1. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.527 vs 0.208), and transformer aggregation was worse than avgpool in the one comparison we have (0.421 vs 0.527). The encoder results show an interaction: ResNet50 worked well with scGPT but poorly with scVI. The biggest remaining uncertainty is profile setting, since all seven experiments used multiprofile. This experiment keeps the best encoders and fusion fixed and switches to singleprofile, which tests whether aggregating multiple profiles is actually needed. It is the best use of the budget because it answers a major design question that has never been tested, while staying close to the leading region. If singleprofile matches or beats 0.653, the search space shifts substantially. If it drops, we can confidently fix multiprofile and spend the remaining budget on refining aggregation and encoders.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Multiprofile beat singleprofile in this setting (0.653 vs 0.532). Weighted fusion clearly beat concat. The only aggregation comparison used the weaker scVI + ViT-L pairing, where the transformer did worse than avgpool (0.421 vs 0.527). Encoder results also show strong interactions: ResNet50 helped with scGPT but not with scVI. So that single transformer result may not carry over to the best encoder pair. 2. What this tests: config_045 changes only the aggregation (transformer instead of avgpool) on the current best configuration. It shows whether the transformer penalty holds generally or whether learned set aggregation helps once the representations are stronger. 3. Why now: Aggregation is the main design choice still uncertain in the leading region. A gain would mean a new best, and a loss would firmly settle on avgpool. Either way the budget then goes to other questions, such as the scGPT RNA-only baseline or the PCA encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is scGPT + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion (0.653 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Other trends are fairly consistent. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in both paired comparisons. Weighted fusion beat concat by a large margin in the one paired test. scGPT beat scVI with both image encoders. The main open question is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, which has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best-performing settings (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about any of the design choices: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_030 is a central anchor point: multimodal, multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, simple concat fusion, the mid-sized scVI RNA encoder and the standard ResNet50 image encoder. It gives a realistic reference score for the full pipeline without using the most complex options. 3) It is the best first use of the budget because every other design question is one change away from it. Each later experiment can isolate a single factor: RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), singleprofile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), ViT-L image encoder (config_036), or PCA/scGPT RNA encoders (config_018/config_042). Starting from a trivial unimodal baseline instead would make later multimodal comparisons less direct.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists. config_030 (multimodal, scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell whether the image branch helps, hurts or does nothing. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder (scVI-200), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but drops the image modality. It is a clean single-factor change, so the result directly estimates how much the ResNet50 image features add over RNA alone. 3. Why now: Whether the study should center on multimodal models is the most consequential and most uncertain design choice. It determines whether later experiments should go to image encoders and fusion methods or to RNA encoders and aggregation. A matched ablation resolves this with one run and gives a reference point for interpreting all later experiments.

1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.411, F1 0.378) performed clearly worse than the matched RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Both used scVI and avgpool. So the current evidence says this way of adding images hurts. It cannot yet tell us whether the image modality is unhelpful or whether naive concatenation lets weak image features swamp the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps every other setting the same. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only performance, the problem was the fusion method and multimodal models are still worth pursuing. If it stays well below RNA-only, that is stronger evidence that ResNet50 images add little. In that case the budget should shift toward RNA-only variants (encoder, aggregation) or a different image encoder. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion is viable decides how the large multimodal part of the search space gets explored. A clean one-factor comparison resolves this efficiently, and it has a plausible chance of improving on the current best.

1) Evidence: with scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, weighted fusion (0.579 acc / 0.563 F1) clearly beat concat (0.411 / 0.378) and RNA-only (0.485 / 0.464). Accuracy and F1 agree, so weighted fusion looks like a real advantage. Aggregation is a major design axis that has not been tested at all: every run so far used avgpool. 2) This experiment changes one variable from the current best (config_031), swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation. It shows whether learned set-level aggregation across profiles adds value on top of weighted fusion. 3) It exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering a key open question cleanly. The result will tell us which aggregator to carry forward before we spend budget on image-encoder (ViT-L) or RNA-encoder (scGPT) variations.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat under the same setup (0.579 vs 0.411 accuracy, with F1 following). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation with weighted fusion (0.579 vs 0.520). The best setup so far, config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), also beats RNA-only (0.485), so adding images helps when fusion is weighted. The main untested choice is the image encoder: every multimodal run used resnet50, so the effect of imagenet_vit_l is unknown. 2. Test: config_037 keeps config_031's settings and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. Any change can therefore be attributed to the encoder. 3. Why now: this exploits the strongest known setup while resolving a major open design choice. It also has a real chance of raising the best score. Changing the RNA encoder (scGPT or PCA) is a natural follow-up once the image backbone question is settled.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.411 accuracy), and F1 agrees. Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.579 vs 0.520). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.536). The best multimodal run also beats RNA-only (0.485). However, every run so far used scVI as the RNA encoder. That makes the RNA encoder the largest unexplored design choice. 2. Test: This run keeps the best-known settings (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for scGPT. Any difference can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone, telling us whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation helps in the strongest pipeline. 3. Why now: The other settings already have reasonable evidence, while the RNA encoder is completely untested and could shift the best result substantially. Testing it inside the best pipeline both explores a new dimension and has a realistic chance of producing a new best configuration. Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.579 accuracy, 0.563 F1). One-factor changes from it were all worse: transformer aggregation (0.520), ViT-L image encoder (0.536), scGPT RNA encoder (0.518) and concat fusion (0.411). Weighted fusion therefore looks important, and the other choices near the best point are partly mapped. The profile setting, however, has never been varied: every run is multiprofile. Test: config_029 keeps config_031 exactly but uses a single profile, isolating whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. Why now: this is a major untested design axis and a clean controlled comparison against the current best. It tells us whether to keep investing in multiprofile variants or whether simpler single-profile models are competitive. PCA RNA encoding is also untested, but the profile setting is the more basic structural choice, so it should be resolved first.

1. Evidence: config_031 is the best result so far (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.579, F1 0.563). Every single-factor change from it has scored lower. Concat fusion gave 0.411, transformer aggregation 0.520, ViT-L image encoder 0.536, scGPT RNA encoder 0.518 and single-profile input 0.471. The one design axis never tested is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder. 2. This experiment keeps the best settings and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. It finishes the one-factor check around the current best. It shows whether the simple PCA representation matches or beats scvi_n200, given that the more complex scGPT encoder did worse. 3. It fills the largest remaining gap with a controlled comparison. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. That makes it better value than further probing settings that already performed poorly.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.619, F1 0.610). Switching the RNA encoder to PCA from scVI improved accuracy by about 0.04. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.411). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and ResNet50 beat ViT-L, but each of those conclusions rests on a single comparison made with the scVI encoder. The image-encoder gap (0.579 vs 0.536) is moderate and could interact with the RNA representation. 2. Test: config_025 keeps the best setup and changes only the image encoder to ViT-L. This shows whether ResNet50's advantage holds on the strongest RNA encoder or was specific to scVI. 3. Why now: it is a single-factor change around the current best, so it is likely to perform competitively while settling an image-encoder choice that currently rests on weak, single-comparison evidence. If ViT-L wins, it opens a new branch to exploit. If it loses, ResNet50 is confirmed and later budget can go to the aggregation question (config_021).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beats the matched scVI run, config_031 (0.579). Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.411). Avgpool beat transformer once (0.579 vs 0.520), but that is a single comparison. With scVI, adding images to the RNA-only baseline raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.579. We do not yet know whether PCA's edge comes from PCA being a better RNA representation or from it fusing better with images. 2. What this tests: config_002 is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool. It is the missing unimodal baseline for the best encoder. Comparing it with config_005 (scVI RNA-only) isolates the RNA-encoder effect without images. Comparing it with config_019 measures how much the image branch adds for PCA. 3. Why now: This single run settles where the current best performance comes from, which is the key uncertainty for later choices. That includes whether a transformer aggregation variant of the best setup (config_021) is worth testing. If PCA alone is strong, later experiments should focus on PCA-based setups. If it is not, the gain comes from fusion, and the search should focus on the image and fusion components instead.

1. There is no evidence yet, so every design choice is open: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. This experiment sets a central anchor point. It is a multimodal, multiprofile model with mid-complexity choices: the compact learned scVI RNA embedding, the strong pretrained ViT-L image encoder, simple avgpool aggregation and plain concat fusion. It sits in the region most likely to perform well, and it is not an extreme on any axis. 3. Under a limited budget, a central anchor lets later experiments change one factor at a time and attribute the effect. Examples are dropping a modality (config_005 or config_014), switching to singleprofile (config_034), or changing to transformer aggregation (config_038), weighted fusion (config_037), scgpt or pca RNA encoders, or resnet50. Starting from the simplest baseline would give less information per experiment.

1. Evidence: only one experiment exists, config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), which reached 0.227 accuracy and 0.191 F1. With a single data point, we have no evidence yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_038 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates how multiple profiles are combined, a major architectural choice that could plausibly give large gains by modeling interactions between profiles. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: a clean single-factor comparison against the existing baseline lets us attribute any change directly to aggregation. It also has real upside for the primary accuracy objective. Modality ablations (RNA-only or image-only) and fusion changes are natural follow-ups once aggregation is settled.

1. Evidence: With scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + concat held fixed, transformer aggregation (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) far outperformed avgpool (0.227 acc, 0.191 F1). Both accuracy and F1 agree, so transformer aggregation looks like a strong design choice for multiprofile models. Fusion strategy, however, is still completely untested. 2. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup and changes only one thing, concat to weighted fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to fusion alone. 3. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction found so far and has a realistic chance of beating the best result. It also resolves an open multimodal design choice that applies to every other encoder pairing, which makes it a good use of a limited budget. Swapping the encoders or running unimodal ablations next, with transformer and the better fusion fixed, would then be well grounded.

1) Evidence: All three runs used scvi_n200 RNA and imagenet_vit_l images. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin (0.485 vs 0.227 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). Concat fusion beat weighted fusion (0.485 vs 0.332). Both gaps are large enough to treat transformer + concat as the working backbone. The RNA encoder has not been varied at all, and it has three options, so it is the largest unexplored design axis. 2) Test: config_050 keeps everything from the best run (config_038: multiprofile, vit_l, transformer, concat) and swaps only scvi_n200 for scGPT. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3) Why now: it varies one factor at a time from the current best, so it is both exploitation and exploration. A pretrained foundation encoder like scGPT has a plausible chance of beating the best result. Even if it does not, the outcome tells us whether RNA representation matters before we spend budget on the image-encoder swap or unimodal ablations.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.485 vs 0.227). Concat beat weighted fusion (0.485 vs 0.332). Switching the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT gave the best result so far (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). Every run so far used imagenet_vit_l, so the image encoder is the one major design choice with no evidence at all. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates the effect of the image encoder in the most promising context. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it fills the largest untested gap in the design space and could also find a better configuration. A large drop would confirm ViT-L as the image encoder to keep. A similar or higher score would show the image encoder matters little or that resnet50 is better, which would shape the remaining budget. Either result is informative.

Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.48 vs 0.23 with scVI/ViT-L). scGPT strongly outperforms scVI (0.63 vs 0.48). ResNet50 beats ViT-L when paired with scGPT (0.715 vs 0.63, with F1 agreeing). Weighted fusion underperformed concat once, but that is a single comparison. The key unresolved question is whether the image modality adds anything at all, since every run so far is multimodal and RNA encoder quality appears to drive most of the gains. Test: config_009 (scGPT, RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) is a direct unimodal ablation of the current best, config_044. If it nears 0.715, images contribute little and the remaining budget should focus on RNA and aggregation choices. If it falls well below, the multimodal gain is confirmed and later runs can refine the image side and fusion (e.g., config_045). Why now: this one run answers the most consequential open design question and guides the rest of the search, which is worth more than another small fusion tweak on the current best.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.485 vs 0.227), and scGPT beats scVI. ResNet50 beats ViT-L as the image encoder with scGPT. However, the best multimodal run (config_044, scGPT+ResNet50+transformer+concat, 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) only matches RNA-only scGPT (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). So it is unclear whether the image modality adds value under concat fusion. Fusion has been compared only once, in a weak setting (scVI+ViT-L), where weighted fusion was worse. That single result may not hold for stronger encoders. Test: config_045 keeps the best multimodal setup and switches to weighted fusion. Weighted fusion can down-weight a weaker image branch, so this checks whether better fusion lets multimodal surpass RNA-only. It also checks whether the concat-over-weighted conclusion holds outside the scVI/ViT-L case. Why now: it targets the top-performing region while resolving the design choice that is both highly uncertain and most relevant to the main question of whether multimodal fusion beats RNA-only.

Evidence: scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.63-0.72 accuracy versus 0.23-0.48 for scVI. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin in the only comparison (0.485 vs 0.227). Concat beat weighted fusion in all three paired tests. RNA-only scGPT with transformer aggregation (0.721 acc, 0.681 F1) roughly matches the best multimodal run (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1). That suggests the RNA profile carries most of the signal. However, every completed run so far used multiprofile, so the profile-setting dimension is completely untested. Test: config_007 runs scGPT RNA-only in singleprofile mode. Compared directly against config_009, it measures how much multiprofile modelling with transformer aggregation contributes beyond a single-profile scGPT baseline. Why now: this is the largest remaining blind spot in the design space, and it uses the strongest known encoder. If singleprofile is competitive, a whole cheaper branch of configurations becomes worth exploring. If it is clearly worse, it confirms that multiprofile plus transformer aggregation is the key choice, and the remaining budget can focus there.

1) Evidence: concat beats weighted fusion in all three paired comparisons. Transformer beats avgpool aggregation, though only in one pair. scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. However, the best multimodal run (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer, concat: 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) only matches the RNA-only scGPT transformer baseline (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). The key open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all, and no image-only run exists yet. 2) This experiment runs ResNet50 image-only with multiprofile transformer aggregation. That is the image counterpart of the best RNA-only setup and uses the better-performing image encoder. It measures how much predictive signal images provide on their own. 3) It is the best use of budget because the answer decides where to spend the remaining runs. If image-only performance is weak, further multimodal fusion tuning is unlikely to pay off, and effort should shift to RNA-side and aggregation choices. If it is reasonably strong, the lack of multimodal gain points to a fusion problem, which justifies exploring fusion and aggregation variants with scGPT + ResNet50.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several design choices look consistent. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.485 vs 0.227). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion in both matched pairs. Multiprofile beats singleprofile for scGPT RNA-only (0.721 vs 0.650). scGPT beats scVI. The best result so far is scGPT RNA-only with a transformer (0.721 acc). It is essentially tied with the scGPT+ResNet50 concat multimodal model (0.715 acc, slightly higher F1), so adding images has not yet clearly helped. The largest unexplored design choice is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been tested in any setting. 2. What this tests: config_003 applies pca_n2000 in the strongest known RNA-only setup (multiprofile, transformer). This isolates the effect of the encoder with no confound from fusion or the image encoder. It will show whether a simple high-dimensional PCA representation can match or beat scGPT. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Repeating minor variants of the scGPT path would add little information. A whole level of the encoder factor is still unknown, and this run fills that gap at low risk. If PCA is competitive, pca_n2000+ResNet50 transformer concat (config_020) becomes the logical follow-up. If it is weak, scGPT is confirmed as the RNA encoder, and the remaining budget can focus on whether multimodal fusion adds value.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open: modality, single vs. multi-profile input, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. The most important open question is whether combining modalities beats either one alone. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple multimodal baseline. It uses the classic encoders (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image), multi-profile input with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), and the simplest fusion (concat). The other factors are kept simple, so the result gives a reference point for overall performance in the multimodal region. Later runs can each change one factor from this anchor: image-only (config_011), RNA-only (config_002), single-profile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and swapping in scVI/scGPT or ViT-L. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting at a reference point with many one-factor neighbors lets each later experiment act as a clean ablation, which helps learn which choices matter. Multimodal, multi-profile inputs are also plausibly high-performing for cellular profiling, though this is an untested prior, so the run serves both exploration and possible early exploitation.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.517 F1. With nothing to compare against, we cannot tell whether the image modality adds anything over RNA alone, and that is the most basic design question in the search. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes only one factor from config_018. It drops the image branch and keeps the PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. The gap between the two runs directly estimates how much ResNet50 images contribute under concat fusion. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: if RNA-only performs about as well, later experiments should focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation rather than on image encoders and fusion. If multimodal clearly wins, it justifies spending budget on image-encoder and fusion variants. 1) Evidence so far: multimodal PCA+ResNet50 with avgpool and concat reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.517 F1. RNA-only PCA with avgpool reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. Adding images therefore gave only a small gain (about 0.02 accuracy and F1), so RNA appears to carry most of the signal. The RNA encoder is still completely untested beyond PCA. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the current best: it swaps PCA for the pretrained scGPT encoder and keeps ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool and concat fusion. Any difference can then be attributed to the RNA representation. 3) Because RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder is likely the highest-leverage design choice left to resolve.
