1) Evidence so far: the best result is multimodal PCA+ResNet50 with avgpool and concat (config_018, acc 0.532, F1 0.517). It only modestly beats RNA-only PCA with avgpool (0.514). scGPT as the RNA encoder performed far worse (0.260), so PCA is the RNA encoder to build on. Aggregation has only ever been tested as avgpool, so how to combine multiple profiles is a major open question. 2) Config_020 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This gives a clean single-variable test of whether learned attention over profiles beats mean pooling. 3) Aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, so the answer will shape the rest of the search. Since this experiment starts from the current best setup, it is also a plausible route to a higher score. The image encoder (ViT-L), fusion type and scVI remain to be tested after this.

Evidence: PCA RNA plus ResNet50 multimodal beats RNA-only with avgpool (0.532 vs 0.514), so the image modality may help slightly. Transformer aggregation gave a clear gain over avgpool (0.591 vs 0.532 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). scGPT performed poorly in the one run that used it. The image encoder has never been varied, and the RNA result shows encoder choice can matter a great deal. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_020: PCA, transformer, concat) and changes only ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates the effect of the image encoder within the strongest setup found so far. Why now: image encoder is a major untested design choice, and this test both explores it and exploits the promising transformer direction. Fusion type (concat vs weighted) is likely a smaller effect and can be tested next on whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion, acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.06 under concat fusion. PCA clearly beat scGPT, and ResNet50 beat ViT-L under transformer aggregation. The fusion choice is the biggest open question: weighted fusion has never been tested, so its effect is completely unknown. 2. Test: config_021 changes only the fusion method on the best configuration, from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: it directly exploits the strongest configuration while closing the largest untested gap in the design space. Either result is useful. It may set a new best, or it will confirm concat and let later experiments focus on the RNA encoder (for example scVI on this setup) or on modality ablations.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. The other variants of that setup all did worse. Switching to avgpool gave 0.532, to ViT-L gave 0.520, and to weighted fusion gave 0.542 with a lower F1. The RNA encoder is the least settled choice. scGPT was much worse than PCA under avgpool (0.260 vs 0.532), and scVI-200 has never been tested. 2. What this tests: config_032 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. That isolates whether a learned, compact latent space can match or beat PCA when paired with the strongest aggregation, image encoder and fusion settings. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder is a high-impact factor, given how badly scGPT did. Testing scVI in the most promising setup either finds a better model or confirms PCA as the RNA encoder, which would let later runs focus on profile setting and the unimodal baselines. Both outcomes are useful under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1). The only modality comparison uses avgpool. There, multimodal (0.532) beat RNA-only (0.514) by just about 2 points. Switching to transformer aggregation added about 6 points for multimodal. So it is unclear whether the gain comes from the image modality or from transformer aggregation over profiles. 2. Test: RNA-only with PCA and transformer aggregation is a direct counterpart to config_020 that removes the image branch. If it scores near 0.59, the image modality adds little and the transformer drives performance. If it stays near 0.51–0.53, fusing images matters specifically when combined with transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: The modality question underlies every later choice, including fusion type, image encoder and whether to keep exploring multimodal configurations. Answering it with one cheap, controlled experiment reduces uncertainty more than another small tweak around the current best.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. The evidence is fairly consistent on three choices. Transformer beats avgpool in both the multimodal and RNA-only settings. PCA beats scVI and scGPT as the RNA encoder. Concat beats weighted fusion. The big untested question is the profile setting: every completed run used multiprofile. 2. Test: config_016 is the singleprofile version of the best encoder and fusion choices (PCA + ResNet50, concat). It shows how much multiprofile aggregation adds over single profiles. That tells us whether the transformer and avgpool gains are real benefits of aggregating multiple profiles, or whether singleprofile is a competitive or even better option. 3. Why now: it settles a high-level design choice that has never been sampled, at low cost and with a clear contrast to the known best model. That is more informative than another small fusion or encoder variation, where the evidence already points in one direction.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA + ResNet50, concat; 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beats every multiprofile run, including the best transformer variant (0.591). But singleprofile has been tested only once, so the gain could come from the singleprofile setting itself or from how the image and RNA features combine under it. In multiprofile, adding images helped somewhat (0.591 vs 0.540 RNA-only with transformer; 0.532 vs 0.514 with avgpool). We do not yet know whether that holds in singleprofile. 2) What this tests: config_001 is the RNA-only singleprofile counterpart to config_016. It gives two controlled comparisons at once. Against config_016, it isolates the image modality's contribution in singleprofile. Against config_002 and config_003 (RNA-only multiprofile), it checks whether the singleprofile advantage appears in a second model setting rather than resting on one run. 3) Why now: Before spending budget refining fusion, image encoder or RNA encoder within singleprofile (e.g., config_017, config_022, config_028), it is more efficient to confirm that singleprofile is genuinely better. We also need to know whether multimodality is the key driver. This single, cheap ablation addresses the two most important open design questions at the same time.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor in the multimodal region. It uses scVI (n200), a widely used mid-complexity RNA encoder, together with the standard ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile input with simple avgpool aggregation, and plain concat fusion. It is a reasonable prior guess for a strong configuration, and each of its components can be changed one at a time in later runs. Those one-factor comparisons would cover RNA encoder (PCA vs scGPT), image encoder (ViT-L), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), profile setting (single) and modality (the rna_only and image_only counterparts). 3. Why it is the best use of the next experiment: Under a limited budget, an anchor near the likely optimum gives a useful performance baseline and lets later runs be read as controlled ablations, instead of starting from an extreme corner of the space.

1) Evidence: only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.427 accuracy and 0.417 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_036 changes one factor, the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the image encoder. 3) Why now: the image encoder splits the multimodal search space in half, so learning its effect early guides many later choices. ViT-L is also a plausible upgrade, so this run combines a clean comparison with a real chance of beating the baseline. Modality ablations and aggregation or fusion variants can follow once the encoder question is clearer.

Evidence: in an otherwise identical setup (scVI RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L dropped accuracy from 0.427 to 0.260, with F1 falling similarly. So the image branch strongly affects performance and can clearly hurt it. We do not yet know whether ResNet50 features add anything beyond RNA, or whether 0.427 mostly comes from the RNA side. Test: config_005 is the RNA-only counterpart of config_030, with the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. It isolates the image modality's contribution. Value: this baseline decides how to spend the remaining budget. If RNA-only matches or beats config_030, multimodal fusion and image encoder choices matter less, and the search should shift toward RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly below, ResNet50-based multimodal setups are confirmed as the direction to exploit, and the next steps would test transformer aggregation (config_032) and weighted fusion (config_031).

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool reached 0.653 accuracy. Adding images with concat fusion dropped this sharply, to 0.427 with ResNet50 and 0.260 with ViT-L. Image features as currently fused appear to add noise that overwhelms the RNA signal. It is unclear whether this harm comes from multimodality itself or from naive concat fusion. 2) config_031 keeps everything identical to config_030 (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and only switches concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion can down-weight the weak image branch, accuracy and F1 should recover toward or beyond the RNA-only baseline. If not, multimodality is likely harmful here. 3) Most remaining configurations are multimodal, so this single controlled comparison decides whether that large region deserves further budget. If it does not, the search can focus on RNA-only variants such as aggregation (config_006) and encoder choice (scGPT, PCA).

1. Evidence: Fusion choice clearly matters. With scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, weighted fusion reached 0.721 accuracy (F1 0.681), while concat reached only 0.427. Weighted fusion is also the only setup that beats RNA-only (0.653), so it appears to be what makes the image modality useful. Aggregation is still completely untested, since every run so far used avgpool. 2. Test: config_033 keeps the best setup (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and changes only avgpool to transformer. Any difference can therefore be attributed to aggregation. 3. Why now: this extends the strongest result found so far while also answering an open question about a major design choice. Testing weighted fusion with ViT-L or other RNA encoders would be useful, but those rank behind it because ViT-L has so far performed poorly.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Fusion is the strongest signal so far. With scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, weighted fusion reached 0.721 accuracy versus 0.427 for concat, and F1 followed the same pattern. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.721 vs 0.573). RNA-only scVI already reaches 0.653, so RNA carries most of the predictive signal. Yet every experiment so far has used scVI, so the RNA encoder choice is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_043 keeps the best pipeline (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for scGPT. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder within the current best setup. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: since RNA drives most of the performance, the RNA encoder is likely a high-impact choice that remains unexplored. This run could produce a new best result, and if it does not, it still tells us whether scVI should stay fixed. That is more valuable than testing ViT-L under weighted fusion, because the image modality appears to contribute less.

Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat. With scVI, ResNet50 and avgpool, accuracy rose from 0.427 with concat (config_030) to 0.721 with weighted (config_031), the best result so far, with F1 0.681. ImageNet ViT-L has been tried only once, with concat (config_036, 0.260). So we cannot tell whether ViT-L is a weak image encoder or whether it simply suffered from concat fusion. Question: config_037 changes only the image encoder relative to the best configuration (scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted). It tests whether the image-encoder choice matters once fusion is done well. Why now: the image encoder is the most confounded of the important design axes. If ViT-L with weighted fusion matches or beats ResNet50, half the remaining multimodal space becomes promising again. If it stays clearly worse, we can confidently drop ViT-L configurations and focus the rest of the budget on the RNA encoder (e.g., PCA) and profile-setting questions around the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Some design choices already look settled. Weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin in both direct comparisons. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and scVI beat scGPT, though each of those rests on a single comparison. The profile setting is the largest open question. Every experiment so far has been multiprofile, so we have no evidence on whether pooling multiple profiles helps compared with a single profile. 2. What this tests: config_029 keeps the strongest known components (scVI, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and switches only to singleprofile. It is therefore a clean single-factor test of whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds value. 3. Why now: This is a major structural design axis with zero data. Resolving it is more informative than further refining encoders or aggregation within the multiprofile setting. Because it uses the best known components, it also keeps a reasonable chance of a competitive result.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Weighted fusion has beaten concat in both paired comparisons, by a large margin. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one test we have. ResNet50 has clearly beaten ViT-L. Among RNA encoders, scVI beat scGPT (0.721 vs 0.632), but the third encoder, PCA (n=2000), has never been tested in any setting, so the RNA encoder choice is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best-known setup (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, multiprofile) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA. This isolates whether scVI's advantage holds against a simple high-dimensional baseline, or whether PCA does as well or better. 3. Why now: This one-factor change fills the only untested level of a key design choice while staying in the high-performing region, so it can both inform the search and possibly improve on the best result. It is more informative than another small refinement of a factor we already have evidence on.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted multimodal setup (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). It beats RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.653 accuracy, 0.628 F1), which suggests images add value. Some design choices already look fairly settled: weighted fusion beat concat in both image-encoder pairs, ResNet50 beat ViT-L, scVI beat scGPT and PCA, and avgpool beat transformer in one test. The big open question is that no image-only baseline has been run, so we don't know how informative ResNet50 image features are on their own. 2. Test: Image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with avgpool shows how much predictive signal the image branch carries alone. That tells us whether the ~7-point multimodal gain comes from strong, complementary image information or only a modest boost. It also helps explain why concat fusion collapsed (0.43), possibly because a weak image modality was drowning out the RNA signal. 3. Why now: The remaining scVI + ResNet50 variants (singleprofile concat, transformer concat) combine choices that have already performed worse, so they are unlikely to beat 0.72 and would teach us little. This baseline fills a key gap in understanding the modality contributions, which will guide how much of the remaining budget to spend on image-side choices versus RNA-side and fusion refinements.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about which design choices matter. The open questions are whether multimodal fusion beats a single modality, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and which encoders work best. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central reference point in the design space. It is multimodal (PCA RNA + ResNet50 image), multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, and uses simple concat fusion. Its encoders and fusion are the simplest options, so it gives a strong but low-complexity baseline that contrasts with many neighbors through one-factor changes: unimodal variants (config_002, config_011), singleprofile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and other encoders (config_030, config_042, config_024). 3) Why it is the best first use of the budget: starting from the middle of the space rather than an extreme corner gives a likely-competitive result. It also makes the following one-factor comparisons as informative as possible for estimating the main effects of modality, profile setting, aggregation, fusion and encoder choice.

1. Evidence: Only one run exists (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479). With one data point, we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. 2. Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates whether learned attention across profiles beats simple averaging. That is a central design question for the multiprofile setting, and the answer carries over to every other encoder and fusion combination. 3. Why now: As a one-factor change, any difference in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to aggregation, which gives a clean answer. It also has a real chance of improving on the current best, so it balances learning with progress. Ablations of modality (e.g., config_002) and comparisons of encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) are natural next steps once the aggregation choice is clearer.

Evidence: in the only controlled comparison so far (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat, multiprofile), transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.20 in accuracy (0.721 vs 0.520), and F1 moved the same way (0.681 vs 0.479). That gap is large enough to treat transformer aggregation as the working default. The other factors (image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion) are still untested. What this tests: config_026 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image backbone improves on the current best. Why now: changing one factor at a time gives clean attribution. The image encoder probably affects representation quality more than the fusion rule, so this experiment could both find a better configuration and settle which backbone to use in later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons.

1) Evidence: Three runs so far. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool with PCA+ResNet50+concat (0.721 vs 0.520 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L under transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.507). Every run used the PCA RNA encoder, so the RNA encoder choice, with three options, is completely unexplored. Fusion type is also untested, but it has only two options and probably a smaller effect. 2) Test: Keep the best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, concat) and swap only the RNA encoder from PCA to the scGPT foundation-model embedding. This isolates whether a pretrained RNA representation improves on PCA. 3) Value: It exploits the strongest known setup while removing the largest remaining uncertainty. scGPT differs most from PCA, so the result is the most informative about whether the RNA encoder matters. Either outcome tells us whether later budget should go to RNA encoders (including scVI) or to fusion tuning.

1. Evidence: config_020 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + transformer + concat) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Each single-factor change from it dropped performance to about 0.51–0.53: avgpool aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder and the scGPT RNA encoder. So transformer aggregation, resnet50 and pca_n2000 each appear to matter. Fusion is the one design axis never varied; every run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_021 changes only fusion (concat to weighted) on the best configuration. This isolates whether weighted fusion helps, hurts or makes no difference. 3. Why now: it is both exploitative, since it may beat 0.721, and informative, since it closes the largest gap in our understanding of the design space with a clean one-factor comparison. That is a better use of one run than trying scVI or unimodal ablations first.

1. Evidence: config_020 (PCA, ResNet50, transformer, concat) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it so far has dropped performance to about 0.51–0.54, with F1 falling in step. Those changes were avgpool aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder, the scGPT RNA encoder and weighted fusion. So these design choices interact strongly, and the full set of 020 settings appears to matter. The main RNA-encoder option not yet tested in this context is scVI. 2. Test: config_032 changes only the RNA encoder in the winning configuration, swapping PCA for scVI. It shows whether PCA is uniquely suited here or whether a compact learned embedding can match or beat it. 3. Why now: this completes the one-factor-at-a-time view around the current best on the remaining open encoder choice. It also has a realistic chance of improving on 020, so it serves both learning and optimization. Modality ablations such as RNA-only or image-only would help explain the result but are less likely to produce a better model, so they can come later.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: All six experiments so far are multimodal. The best is config_020 (PCA_n2000 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it fell to 0.51-0.58: avgpool instead of transformer, ViT-L instead of ResNet50, scGPT or scVI instead of PCA, and weighted instead of concat fusion. Because config_020 sits well above all its neighbours, it could be a real optimum or partly noise. We also have no unimodal baselines, so we cannot tell how much the image branch contributes. 2. What this tests: config_003 is RNA-only with the same PCA_n2000 encoder, multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation as the best run. Comparing it with config_020 isolates whether adding ResNet50 image features actually improves results. If RNA-only scores close to 0.72, the RNA representation and transformer aggregation drive performance, and further image-encoder or fusion tuning is low priority. If it scores well below, multimodal fusion is confirmed as important. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Testing more neighbours of config_020 would mostly confirm that those changes hurt. Whether multimodality is worth it is the most important untested design question, and answering it with one matched ablation will guide how the remaining budget is spent.

1. Evidence: config_020 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + transformer + concat) is the clear leader at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it dropped performance to about 0.51–0.58: avgpool aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder, scGPT or scVI RNA encoders, and weighted fusion. The RNA-only version with the same pca + transformer setup reached only 0.514. So the 0.72 result is either a real synergy or partly an outlier, and we have no image-only baseline to tell which. 2. Test: config_012 runs resnet50 + transformer on images alone (image_only, multiprofile). If it scores near 0.72, the image pathway drives performance and RNA adds little. If it scores near 0.5, the multimodal combination is responsible for the gain. 3. Why now: modality contribution is the most important unresolved design question. The answer decides whether the remaining budget should go to refining RNA encoders and fusion, or to the image and aggregation side.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Single-factor changes from it all scored lower, mostly by large margins: avgpool aggregation 0.520, ViT-L image encoder 0.507, scGPT RNA 0.525, weighted fusion 0.537 and scVI RNA 0.579. Image-only ResNet50 with transformer aggregation reached 0.678, so adding RNA gives a modest gain over images alone. The one design dimension still completely untested is the profile setting: every completed experiment used multiprofile. 2. Test: config_016 is identical to config_020 except that it uses singleprofile, with no aggregation. It cleanly measures how much multiprofile input with transformer aggregation contributes over a single profile. The large avgpool-versus-transformer gap suggests the aggregation step matters a lot, but we cannot yet tell whether multiprofile helps or whether avgpool simply hurts. 3. Why now: This is a one-factor-away ablation of the current best on the only unexplored major axis. It closes the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space at the cost of a single experiment, which suits the limited budget. If singleprofile turns out competitive, the singleprofile branch becomes worth exploring; if not, multiprofile with transformer aggregation is confirmed as the core design choice.

Evidence: the two strongest results are close. config_020 (multiprofile, transformer, concat, pca_n2000 + resnet50) reached 0.721 accuracy, and config_016 (singleprofile, concat, pca_n2000 + resnet50) reached 0.715 accuracy with a slightly higher F1. In the multiprofile transformer setting, single changes to the RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion or aggregation caused large and somewhat erratic drops (0.51-0.58). That makes the transformer regime look sensitive, so each of those comparisons is weak evidence. The RNA encoder effect rests on one comparison: scvi_n200 scored 0.579 versus 0.721 for pca. Across RNA encoders, scvi_n200 has been the stronger alternative to pca. Test: config_028 swaps pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 in the simpler, near-best singleprofile concat + resnet50 setup. This checks whether the RNA encoder ranking holds outside the sensitive transformer setting, with everything else matched to config_016. Why now: it is a one-variable comparison against a strong baseline and has a realistic chance of beating the current best. It also clarifies whether scvi's earlier deficit reflects the encoder itself or an interaction with transformer aggregation. That makes it more informative per experiment than further changes in the unstable multiprofile regime or weak RNA-only and ViT runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multi-profile input, encoder type, aggregation method, or fusion method. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central reference point. It is multimodal (PCA RNA + ResNet50 image), uses multiple profiles, and pairs the simplest aggregation (avgpool) with the simplest fusion (concat). Each later experiment can change one factor from this point: drop a modality (vs. config_002/011), switch to a single profile (vs. config_016), swap in a stronger encoder (scGPT, scVI, ViT-L), or try transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: An anchor near the middle of the design space makes later single-factor comparisons cleaner than starting at an extreme. It is also a reasonable bet for good performance, since combining modalities and profiles is plausibly helpful. Using the cheaper, simpler components first means later gains from more complex components can be attributed to them rather than confounded.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; config_018) reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.517 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell which parts of the design drive this result. The most basic open question is whether adding the image modality helps at all. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the same RNA encoder (PCA), the same multiprofile setting and the same avgpool aggregation, but drops the image branch. This makes it a clean one-factor ablation of the image modality. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.532, the image branch adds little and later experiments should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly short, multimodal fusion is justified, and swapping in a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or changing fusion becomes the logical next step. 3. Why now: Whether to use both modalities determines the structure of most of the remaining search space. Answering it early, with a controlled comparison, reduces the most uncertainty per experiment before we spend budget tuning finer choices.

1. Evidence: The multimodal concat model with PCA RNA, ResNet50 and avgpool (0.532 accuracy, 0.517 F1) only slightly beats the matched RNA-only model (0.520, 0.498). The image branch therefore adds a small, uncertain gain, and with one run each we cannot tell whether images are weakly informative or the ResNet50 features are just a weak representation. 2. Test: config_024 keeps everything identical to the best run (PCA RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. Comparing the two isolates the effect of image encoder quality on multimodal performance. 3. Why now: Image encoder is a major, untested design axis, and this one-factor change is both informative and a plausible improvement. A clear gain would show that image features matter and point the search toward stronger image backbones. No gain would suggest RNA dominates, so later experiments should focus on the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) and aggregation choices.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal PCA + ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion (acc 0.532, F1 0.517). It is only slightly above RNA-only PCA (0.520 / 0.498), so the image branch adds a little at best. Swapping in ViT-L under concat dropped accuracy to 0.224, well below RNA-only. That suggests naive concatenation lets a poor image representation degrade the model. Fusion type is therefore a key open design choice, and it has not been tested yet. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. It cleanly isolates the effect of fusion. Weighted fusion may let the model balance RNA and image contributions, turning the marginal image gain into a clearer one. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it both exploits the leading configuration and resolves an important uncertainty with a single-variable change. If weighted fusion helps, it supports testing weighted fusion on the ViT-L arm (config_025) and on other RNA encoders. If it does not, the search can turn to aggregation (transformer) or the RNA encoder instead.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion is the clearest signal so far. config_019 (weighted, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) beat config_018 (concat, 0.532 / 0.517), and it was the only multimodal run that clearly beat RNA-only (0.520). With concat fusion, ResNet50 did far better than ViT-L (0.532 vs 0.224). Aggregation is completely untested: every run so far used avgpool. 2) Test: config_021 keeps the best setup (PCA RNA, ResNet50, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation and is a natural extension of the strongest result. 3) Why now: aggregation affects most of the remaining multimodal and unimodal configurations, so settling it early is worth more than refining smaller choices. Running it on the current best base means one result both reduces uncertainty and could become the new best. Testing ViT-L or other RNA encoders can come after the aggregation choice is clearer.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Weighted fusion clearly beat concat at fixed settings (0.721 vs 0.532), and transformer aggregation came in lower (0.629). The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis: every run so far used pca_n2000, and RNA-only PCA already reached 0.520. 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps the best-performing setup (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation improves or hurts the strongest multimodal model. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it exploits the most promising configuration while reducing uncertainty about a major untested choice. The result will also show whether scVI or scGPT variants deserve more of the limited budget. Testing whether weighted fusion rescues ViT-L (config_025) is a lower priority, because ViT-L performed very poorly (0.224) and weighted fusion may simply down-weight it.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat. With the PCA, ResNet50 and avgpool backbone, accuracy was 0.721 versus 0.532, and F1 agreed. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.629). Among RNA encoders, PCA beat scVI (0.721 vs 0.579). The ViT-L image encoder did badly, but it was only tested with concat. The biggest open question is the scGPT RNA encoder, which has never been tried in any setting. 2) This run keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps in scGPT. That isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA encoder beats PCA. 3) This is the best use of the budget for two reasons. It explores the only RNA encoder with no data at all. It also stays in the most promising region, so it could produce a new best result. Checking whether ViT-L recovers with weighted fusion seems less promising, given how far behind it was (0.224).

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.53). PCA beat scVI (0.58) and scGPT (0.52). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.63). However, every experiment so far has used multiprofile. Whether aggregating multiple profiles helps at all is a major design choice that remains completely untested. 2) What this tests: config_017 matches the best configuration exactly, except that it uses singleprofile. This isolates the value of multiprofile aggregation in the strongest known setting. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It resolves uncertainty about an entire untested dimension with one clean controlled comparison. The outcome will show whether later budget should go to the multiprofile or the singleprofile branch. It also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best, so it is exploratory but not wasteful.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat with PCA+ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.532 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). PCA_n2000 is the best RNA encoder tested so far. Single-profile and multi-profile perform about the same (0.725 vs 0.721). The image encoder remains unresolved: ImageNet ViT-L was only tried with concat fusion, where it collapsed (0.224). That failure may reflect the poor fusion method rather than the encoder. 2. Test: config_025 swaps ViT-L into the best-known multi-profile setup (PCA, avgpool, weighted fusion). This directly tests whether ViT-L's poor result was caused by concat fusion or by the encoder itself, changing only the image encoder relative to config_019. 3. Value: The image encoder choice governs about half of the remaining search space. If ViT-L stays poor under weighted fusion, all ViT-L configurations can be deprioritized and the budget focused on ResNet50 refinements. If it recovers or beats ResNet50, it opens a promising new direction. This controlled comparison is worth more than a small exploitative tweak to the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: weighted fusion with PCA and ResNet50 is the clear winner so far, at 0.725 accuracy single-profile (config_017) and 0.721 multi-profile (config_019). Concat fusion did consistently worse, and RNA-only reached only 0.520 (config_002). The two profile settings score about the same. What remains unknown is how much of the ~0.72 comes from the image branch alone. 2. What this tests: the image-only ResNet50 single-profile baseline measures that directly. If it scores near 0.72, the RNA branch adds little, and comparing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) is low value. If it scores well below 0.72, multimodal fusion is confirmed as the key design choice, and later experiments should refine the RNA encoder and fusion within the weighted, single-profile setup. 3. Why now: it is a single cheap baseline that settles the most basic design question, which modality carries the signal. That steers how the rest of the limited budget is spent better than another small variation near the current best.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or the choice of encoder matters. 2) config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is a central anchor built from the simplest choice in every dimension. Its result will be a reference point for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons later: it can be paired with unimodal runs (config_002, config_011), single-profile runs (config_016), stronger encoders (scGPT, ViT-L), transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion. 3) With a limited budget, a simple baseline that touches every major design axis (both modalities, multiple profiles) gives the most reusable reference for later ablations. It still has a reasonable chance of performing well, rather than spending the first run on a narrow unimodal setup or the most complex combination.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile pipeline (PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell how much of that comes from RNA and how much from imaging. 2) Test: this runs the exact RNA-only counterpart, keeping the same PCA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. It isolates one factor: whether adding the ResNet50 image branch helps at all. 3) Why now: modality is the most basic design choice, and its answer shapes the rest of the search. If RNA alone nearly matches 0.632, the image branch adds little, and the budget is better spent on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. If accuracy drops clearly, imaging carries signal, and improving the image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion becomes the priority. A single controlled ablation gives more direction per experiment than an unanchored encoder swap.

1. Evidence: Only two runs exist. With pca_n2000 RNA and avgpool aggregation held fixed, adding resnet50 images with concat fusion raised accuracy from 0.507 to 0.632, and F1 rose similarly. Image information therefore appears to drive most of the gain. Which image encoder works best is still completely untested, and it is likely a high-impact choice. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l) and keeps everything else in the best configuration fixed. Any difference can be attributed cleanly to the image encoder. 3. Why now: This both exploits and explores. It builds on the strongest result so far, which could raise the top score, while settling a major design choice. Aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder likely matter less given the current evidence, so testing them can wait. An image-only control is also useful, but it would not improve the best result and can be run later.

1) Evidence so far: the ResNet50 + PCA multimodal model with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. That is well above RNA-only (0.507) and the ViT-L multimodal variant (0.512). This points to ResNet50 as the stronger image encoder and suggests image information adds value. Aggregation is still untested: every run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether learned set aggregation helps on multiprofile inputs. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone. 3) This exploits the most promising backbone while resolving a structural choice that affects many of the remaining configurations. The result tells us whether later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons should use avgpool or transformer aggregation, which is a better use of the budget than broader, less controlled exploration.

1) Evidence so far: multimodal beats RNA-only by about 12 accuracy points, so the image modality clearly adds value. ResNet50 beats ViT-L by about 12 points, a strong and consistent signal. Transformer aggregation is modestly better than avgpool (0.653 vs 0.632 accuracy, with F1 agreeing), but that rests on a single comparison. All runs so far used the pca_n2000 RNA encoder and concat fusion, so the RNA encoder choice is completely unexplored and could matter a lot. 2) This run keeps the best-known setup (ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps the RNA encoder to the pretrained scGPT. That isolates the RNA encoder effect against our strongest baseline, config_020. 3) The RNA encoder is the largest remaining source of uncertainty, and the large gap between RNA-only and multimodal suggests the RNA representation may be a bottleneck. Fusion type (weighted vs concat) is likely a smaller effect and can be tested afterward. Running this in the current best context also gives a realistic chance of beating 0.653, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

Evidence so far: ResNet50 clearly beats ViT-L (0.63 vs 0.51 with PCA/avgpool/concat), so image encoder choice matters a lot. Transformer aggregation gives a modest gain over avgpool (0.653 vs 0.632). scGPT beats PCA under the best setting (0.688 vs 0.653), with F1 agreeing. Fusion is completely untested, because every multimodal run used concat. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_044: scGPT, ResNet50, transformer, multiprofile) and changes only fusion to weighted. That isolates the effect of the one design dimension we know nothing about. It is the best use of the next run because it reduces uncertainty about a whole axis that applies to every multimodal configuration. It also has a reasonable chance of becoming the new best result, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. Testing scVI or more ViT variants would add less new information.

1. Evidence: ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L in the matched comparison (0.632 vs 0.512 accuracy). Transformer aggregation modestly beat avgpool (0.653 vs 0.632). scGPT improved on PCA (0.688 vs 0.653), and weighted fusion added a further gain (0.721, F1 0.681). The scVI RNA encoder is still completely untested, so the RNA encoder choice is only partly resolved. 2. Test: config_033 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps only scGPT for scVI. This isolates whether scGPT is truly the best RNA encoder or whether the compact scVI embedding matches or beats it. 3. Why now: it exploits the strongest known pipeline, so it has a real chance of improving the best result. It also resolves the largest remaining unexplored axis in a single controlled comparison. That is a better use of budget than refining fusion with PCA, or revisiting ViT-L, which has already performed poorly.

Evidence: every multimodal run so far is multiprofile. The best result is scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted fusion (config_045, 0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Encoder and fusion choices have had some testing: scGPT beat PCA and scVI, ResNet50 beat ViT-L, the transformer beat avgpool, and weighted beat concat. The profile setting has never been varied, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed. This experiment keeps the best configuration and changes only to singleprofile. If accuracy drops clearly, multiprofile is a key ingredient and the remaining budget can focus on refining it. If accuracy stays similar, a simpler model works as well and the earlier aggregation gains need re-reading. It is the best next use of the budget because it tests a completely unexplored, high-level design choice in the strongest setting, and it could still be competitive in performance.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_045 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.721, F1 0.681). The ImageNet ViT-L image encoder has been tested only once, in a weak setting (PCA RNA, avgpool, concat; 0.512 vs 0.632 for ResNet50 in the same setup). That single run is weak grounds for dropping an entire image-encoder branch. The encoder may interact with the stronger scGPT RNA encoder, the transformer aggregation or the weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_051 keeps every component of the current best configuration and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. Its result directly isolates the image-encoder effect in the most relevant context. 3) Why now: The image encoder is the least-resolved major design axis. Fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder each already have at least one comparison. This run either confirms ResNet50, letting us prune all remaining ViT-L configurations, or gives a new best if ViT-L benefits from weighted fusion. That makes it both informative and a reasonable bet for exploitation.

Evidence: the best results come from scGPT with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion (0.721 with ResNet50, 0.715 with ViT-L). The image encoder seems to matter little in this region. The only test of aggregation (transformer 0.653 vs avgpool 0.632) used PCA with concat fusion, so we don't know if transformer aggregation still matters with the stronger scGPT encoder and weighted fusion. This experiment changes only the aggregation (avgpool instead of transformer), keeping scGPT, ResNet50 and weighted fusion. It shows whether transformer aggregation is needed in the top-performing region or whether a simpler pooling performs as well. That clarifies a key design choice next to the current best, so it is both exploratory and relevant to exploitation. This is a better use of the limited budget than another fusion or encoder swap, where the evidence is already more consistent.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about any design axis: modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple reference point. It is multimodal, uses multiprofile inputs with avgpool aggregation, pairs the simplest encoders (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for images), and fuses by concatenation. Its result sets a baseline that later one-factor changes can be compared against. Each of those comparisons isolates a single question: unimodal vs. multimodal (config_002 or config_011), singleprofile vs. multiprofile (config_016), avgpool vs. transformer (config_020), concat vs. weighted fusion (config_019), and simple vs. pretrained encoders (configs 030/042 for RNA, config_024 for images). 3. Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting from a low-complexity anchor near the middle of the design space makes later comparisons easy to interpret. Its expected performance is also reasonable, since it uses both modalities and multiple profiles. Starting at an extreme, such as the most complex scGPT + ViT-L transformer setup, would confound several factors at once and give less diagnostic value.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.421 accuracy and 0.412 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell how much each modality contributes to that score. 2) What this tests: config_002 keeps the same RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation but removes the image branch. This is a clean one-factor ablation of the image modality. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.421, images add little at this stage. The search should then focus on RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT and on aggregation. If RNA-only drops clearly, multimodal fusion is valuable, and testing image encoders and fusion choices becomes a priority. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: whether to use multimodal models at all is the most basic design choice. Settling it first decides where later experiments should go across most of the remaining configurations. A controlled ablation also gives more interpretable information than changing several factors at once.

1) Evidence: Adding ResNet50 images to PCA RNA with concat fusion (config_018) cut validation accuracy from 0.540 to 0.421, and F1 dropped similarly (0.524 to 0.412). Two explanations remain: the image features add noise, or concat fusion lets a weak modality swamp the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_019 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) and keeps the RNA encoder, image encoder and avgpool aggregation fixed. If weighted fusion recovers to RNA-only accuracy or beats it, fusion was the problem and multimodal models are still worth pursuing. If it stays near 0.42, the ResNet50 image features themselves are probably harmful. 3) Why now: most of the remaining configurations are multimodal and split on fusion type. Settling whether weighted fusion avoids the multimodal penalty therefore decides whether to spend the budget on multimodal models or on RNA-only encoder and aggregation choices.

1. Evidence: The only RNA-only run (config_002, PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) is clearly best, at 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. Adding ResNet50 images under the same settings hurt substantially: 0.421 with concat fusion and 0.327 with weighted fusion. So the RNA branch currently carries the signal. However, only one RNA encoder (PCA) has been tested, so the effect of the RNA representation is unknown. 2. Test: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT embeddings, and keeps rna_only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This cleanly measures whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest direction (RNA-only) while resolving a major untested design axis that every multimodal configuration also depends on. Its result will guide later choices of RNA encoder for both unimodal and fused models, which is more informative than tuning fusion or image settings that have so far only hurt.

1) Evidence: RNA-only models are the strongest so far. scGPT reached 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1, versus 0.540 accuracy for PCA. Adding resnet50 images through concat or weighted fusion clearly hurt performance (0.42 and 0.33 accuracy). Every run so far used avgpool aggregation, so the aggregation choice is completely unexplored. 2) This experiment changes only the aggregation of the current best setup (scGPT RNA-only, multiprofile), from avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles improves on simple mean pooling. 3) Aggregation is a major design axis that affects every multiprofile branch, including later multimodal runs, so this result informs many remaining configurations. It also builds directly on the best-performing setup, giving both new information and a good chance of a new best score. The image-encoder question (resnet50 vs ViT-L) is better tested after the RNA-side design is settled.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models are clearly strongest so far, with scGPT plus avgpool at 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Adding ResNet50 image features to PCA RNA hurt performance badly. Accuracy fell from 0.540 to 0.421 with concat fusion and to 0.328 with weighted fusion. No image-only model has been tested yet, so we cannot tell whether the image modality has little signal or whether ResNet50 features specifically are weak or noisy. 2. Test: an image-only ImageNet ViT-L model under the same multiprofile avgpool setting measures how much predictive signal a stronger image encoder carries on its own. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the result decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth exploring. If ViT-L image-only performs well, scGPT plus ViT-L multimodal configs become promising. If it performs poorly, the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices such as scVI encoders and single- versus multi-profile settings. This answers an uncertainty that affects many remaining configurations, rather than making a small exploitation step.

Evidence: the only multimodal runs so far paired pca_n2000 with resnet50, and both scored below RNA-only pca_n2000 (0.421 concat and 0.328 weighted, vs 0.540). Concat beat weighted. The strongest unimodal results are scGPT RNA-only with avgpool (0.573 acc, 0.573 F1) and ViT-L image-only with avgpool (0.532). This makes it unclear whether multimodal fusion is inherently harmful here or whether the earlier failures came from weaker encoders (pca and resnet50; resnet50 image-only is untested). This experiment fuses the two best encoders, scGPT and ViT-L, keeping avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, the better choices observed so far. If it beats 0.573, fusion adds value with strong encoders, which is the most promising direction. If it still falls below RNA-only scGPT, that is stronger evidence that fusion hurts in this setup, and remaining budget should go to unimodal refinement. It combines exploiting the best known components with resolving the most important open question: whether multimodal is worth pursuing.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. It clearly beats both unimodal baselines (scGPT RNA-only 0.573, ViT-L image-only 0.532), so the scGPT/ViT-L/avgpool/concat setup is a strong base. Single results suggest weighted fusion (0.33 vs 0.42 concat with PCA/ResNet) and transformer aggregation (0.54 vs 0.57 avgpool with scGPT RNA-only) both hurt, though each rests on one comparison. The largest open question is the RNA encoder: scVI has never been tested in any setting, and we only know scGPT slightly beats PCA in RNA-only runs (0.573 vs 0.540). Test: config_036 keeps the winning setup (ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps only scGPT for scVI. This isolates whether scVI can match or beat scGPT in the strongest multimodal context. Why now: it explores a completely unexamined encoder while staying inside the most promising region of the search space, so it could plausibly set a new best result. It is also more informative than re-testing fusion or aggregation options that already look weaker.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat), at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Fusion and aggregation already have some signal. Concat beat weighted for PCA+ResNet50 (0.42 vs 0.33). Avgpool beat transformer for scGPT RNA-only (0.57 vs 0.54, with a larger gap in F1). Profile setting has no signal at all: all eight experiments used multiprofile. 2) This run keeps the best encoder pair and concat fusion and switches only to singleprofile. It isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles actually drives the strong multimodal result, or whether a single profile does as well or better. 3) Profile setting is the largest untested design dimension and affects about half of the search space, so one controlled comparison on the strongest configuration gives the most information per experiment. It also stays near the current best, so it may still produce a competitive result.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. It clearly beats both unimodal baselines (scGPT RNA-only 0.573, ViT-L image-only 0.532) and its single-profile counterpart (0.599). Multiprofile, scGPT and ViT-L therefore look like the right choices. Fusion strategy is still poorly understood. The only weighted-vs-concat comparison used the weak PCA + ResNet50 backbone (0.421 concat vs 0.328 weighted), and that single, low-performing pair may not transfer to stronger encoders. 2. This experiment changes only the fusion method on the best configuration, so it is a controlled test of whether weighted fusion helps or hurts when both modalities are informative. 3. Fusion is a core design choice for multimodal models, and the current evidence on it is the weakest of the remaining open choices. This run exploits the strongest region of the search space while reducing that uncertainty, and the result guides all remaining multimodal runs. Transformer aggregation (config_050) is the natural next follow-up.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about which design choices matter. These include modality (RNA, image, or both), single vs. multi-profile input, encoder type, aggregation, and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple reference point. It is multimodal with multiprofile input, uses the simplest encoders (PCA RNA and ResNet50 image), and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat). Each later experiment can change one factor from this baseline: drop a modality (config_002 or config_011), switch to single-profile (config_016), use transformer aggregation (config_020), use weighted fusion (config_019), or swap in a stronger encoder such as scGPT or ViT-L. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, starting from a mid-complexity baseline allows clean one-factor-at-a-time comparisons for the highest-level choices. It also has a reasonable chance of performing well already. Starting at an extreme, such as the simplest single-modality model or the most complex combination, would make the follow-up comparisons harder to interpret.

1. Evidence: there is only one completed result. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. Its absolute level gives no information about which components are responsible for that performance. 2. What this tests: config_002 drops only the image branch. It keeps the same PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This gives a clean one-factor ablation of whether the image modality, and therefore fusion, adds value over RNA alone. 3. Why now: the modality question decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If RNA-only matches or beats the multimodal result, further work on image encoders and fusion types is unlikely to pay off, and effort should shift to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it clearly underperforms, multimodal exploration is justified, and the next tests should vary the image encoder, RNA encoder or aggregation.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The two completed runs share the same PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (0.536 acc, 0.516 F1) did not beat RNA alone (0.540 acc, 0.524 F1). The gap is small and could be noise, so it is unclear whether the image modality carries little signal or whether concat fusion fails to use it. 2) What this tests: An image-only run with the same ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool settings completes a clean three-way ablation (RNA-only, image-only, fused). It shows how much signal images carry on their own. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: Most of the remaining search space is multimodal. If image-only performs near chance, the budget should shift to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it performs reasonably well, the fusion method and image encoder (weighted fusion, ViT-L) become the key levers to test next.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (pca_n2000, avgpool) reached 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. Image-only resnet50 was much weaker at 0.471. Adding resnet50 images via concat gave 0.536, no better than RNA alone. So RNA carries most of the signal, and the RNA encoder has only been tested with PCA. 2. This run swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT, keeping multiprofile and avgpool fixed. That makes it a controlled comparison with config_002 on what is likely the most influential design choice: a pretrained foundation-model embedding versus a linear PCA embedding. 3. Since RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder choice will shape every later multimodal configuration. Settling it early, before spending budget on image encoder, fusion or aggregation variants, is the most informative use of the next experiment. It also has a real chance of improving on the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Among completed runs, PCA RNA-only with avgpool is the strongest (0.540 acc, 0.524 F1). Multimodal concat with ResNet50 did not improve on it (0.536). Image-only (0.471) and scGPT (0.427) are clearly weaker. Every run so far used avgpool, so we know nothing about whether transformer aggregation over multiple profiles helps. That choice affects almost every multiprofile configuration still available. 2. What this tests: config_003 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) on the best-performing setup. That gives a clean, controlled read on this design axis. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The aggregation result will guide many later choices across unimodal and multimodal configurations. Because it builds on the current best setup, it is also a reasonable bet for immediate gains. Fusion type, scVI and ViT-L are also open questions, but they are best tested once the aggregation choice is better understood.

Evidence: the clearest signal so far is aggregation. Switching RNA-only pca_n2000 from avgpool to transformer raised accuracy from 0.540 to 0.678, with F1 rising from 0.524 to 0.646. With avgpool, multimodal concat (0.536) performed about the same as RNA-only (0.540), so adding resnet50 images showed no benefit. Image-only (0.471) and scGPT RNA-only (0.427) were weaker. Question: config_020 keeps the multimodal concat setup and changes only the aggregation to transformer. This tests whether the transformer gain carries over to the fused model, and whether images add value once a stronger aggregator is used. Comparing it with config_003 isolates whether adding the image modality helps. Comparing it with config_018 shows whether the transformer effect holds across model settings. Why now: it builds on the strongest effect found so far while resolving the main open question of whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. That answer will decide how much of the remaining budget should go to the many multimodal configurations versus RNA-only refinements such as the scVI encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only with PCA and transformer aggregation (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Transformer aggregation gave a large gain for RNA-only (+0.14 over avgpool). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion did not help under avgpool (0.536 vs 0.540). Under transformer aggregation, concat fusion collapsed to 0.332. Image-only is weak (0.471). The open uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion is harmful in itself or whether naive concat is the problem, for example by letting weaker or noisy image features dominate or destabilize transformer training. 2) Test: config_021 keeps everything from the collapsed config_020 (PCA, ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly isolates the fusion choice in the best-performing aggregation regime. If weighted fusion recovers to RNA-only level or beyond, multimodal remains a viable direction and fusion becomes a key design factor. If it also fails, adding images under transformer aggregation is likely harmful, and the budget should shift toward RNA-encoder and RNA-only refinements. 3) Why now: this single controlled comparison decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space deserves further budget. That makes it more informative than marginal RNA-only variations at this stage.

1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation is the strongest signal so far. It raised RNA-only PCA from 0.540 to 0.678 accuracy, with F1 rising in step, and RNA-only PCA + transformer is the current best. Multimodal runs have not beaten it. Concat fusion with a transformer collapsed (0.332), and weighted fusion reached only 0.635. The RNA encoder looks like a major factor, since scGPT was much worse than PCA under avgpool, but scVI has never been tested. 2. Question: Swapping PCA for scVI under the best-known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) isolates whether scVI is a better RNA representation. 3. Why this experiment: It exploits the strongest direction while closing the biggest untested gap in a high-leverage design choice. The result also guides which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal and weighted-fusion experiments, instead of spending budget on more image or fusion variants that have so far lagged.

Evidence: transformer aggregation is the strongest design choice so far. RNA-only PCA with a transformer (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) beats avgpool (0.540). Among multimodal transformer runs, weighted fusion (0.635) far outperformed concat (0.332), so weighted fusion looks necessary when adding images. Multimodal still trails RNA-only. One reason may be the weak ResNet50 image features, since image-only avgpool reached only 0.471. The alternative image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) is completely untested. This experiment keeps the best-supported settings (PCA RNA, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to ViT-L. That isolates whether a stronger image representation lets multimodal fusion match or beat the RNA-only best. It is the best use of the budget because it builds on the promising transformer-plus-weighted direction while resolving a major open question (the image encoder choice). Either outcome is informative: a gain shows multimodal is worth pursuing with ViT-L, and no gain suggests the image modality adds little beyond PCA RNA.

1) Evidence: Every completed run used the multiprofile setting. The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with transformer aggregation (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1), clearly ahead of PCA with avgpool (0.540). Adding images has not helped. Weighted fusion reached 0.635, and concat with a transformer collapsed to 0.332. So aggregation matters, but whether multiprofile input helps at all is untested. 2) Test: config_001 runs the best RNA encoder (PCA) on a single profile with no aggregation. This gives a baseline for the profile-setting decision. If it scores near or above the avgpool result, the gain comes from transformer aggregation rather than from multiple profiles.
